explicacion.es: El eco repite el auxiliar de la frase original: lives → does. Usar siempre is no suena a eco.

erroresFrecuentes.incorrecto: You've met my colleague, no?
erroresFrecuentes.correcto: You've met my colleague, haven't you?

explicacion.es: «¿No?» es un calco del español. La tag copia el auxiliar con polaridad contraria: have → haven't you?

texto.es: En una charla informal, el inglés casi nunca contesta con un simple «yes» o «no»: devuelve un eco. El eco repite el auxiliar de la frase, con su pronombre y la misma polaridad (I've joined… → Have you?; She didn't call → Didn't she?). No pide información: muestra interés o sorpresa y suele ir seguido de un comentario. No lo confundas con la question tag (You've met him, haven't you?), que invierte la polaridad y pide confirmar lo que ya crees. El tono cuenta: un eco sin seguimiento puede sonar frío.
Afirmación + eco + pregunta:

nota.es: afirmación con auxiliar (have)
eco: mismo auxiliar + pronombre; muestra interés
pregunta breve que mantiene viva la charla

titulo.es: Cabeza y cola en la charla oral

texto.es: En la conversación oral, el inglés saca el tema de la frase. Con la cabeza (head) el tema va primero y un pronombre lo retoma: My brother, he's a cook. Con la cola (tail) la frase completa va primero y el tema se añade al final, a menudo para evaluar o aclarar: He's a cook, my brother. En español puedes omitir el sujeto; en inglés el pronombre es obligatorio y concuerda con el tema (sister → she, neighbours → they, film → it). Son recursos del habla informal: en un texto formal no se usan.
Cabeza + pronombre + comentario:

nota.es: cabeza: el tema de la charla
pronombre obligatorio que retoma el tema
comentario sobre el tema

titulo.es: Réplicas cortas: lo omitido y lo sustituido

texto.es: Cuando contestas rápido, no repites lo que el otro ya dijo. Hay tres recursos. Uno: dejar solo to (I'd love to = I'd love to come). Dos: So/Neither + auxiliar + sujeto para «yo también / yo tampoco»; el auxiliar copia el de la frase original (am, do, did, have, can…). Tres: sustituir la oración entera con so o not (I hope so, I think so, I hope not, I'm afraid not). Para entender una réplica, busca el auxiliar y reconstruye el verbo que falta en la frase anterior.

nota.es: frase original con el auxiliar didn't
yo tampoco (se usa tras una frase negativa)
auxiliar copiado + sujeto nuevo; el verbo se omite

Every family dinner in our house follows the same pattern. Somebody begins with a serious subject, like the landlord or the price of flights, and within two minutes my aunt has drifted off into a story about her neighbour's dog. “Anyway,” my father says, always in the same tired voice, “where were we?” By then, of course, nobody remembers. texto.es: Los marcadores de discurso guían la conversación y suelen ir al inicio de la réplica, seguidos de coma. By the way y speaking of cambian de tema (el primero, algo que se te ocurre; el segundo, enlazando con lo dicho). Anyway vuelve al tema principal. To be honest da una opinión sincera sin sonar brusco; mind you matiza lo que acabas de decir. Come to think of it marca un recuerdo repentino y on second thoughts un cambio de opinión. Usa pocos: si los repites en cada frase, suenas ensayado.

items.audio: Every family dinner in our house follows the same pattern. Somebody begins with a serious subject, like the landlord or the price of flights, and within two minutes my aunt has drifted off into a story about her neighbour's dog. “Anyway,” my father says, always in the same tired voice, “where were we?” By then, of course, nobody remembers. Come to think of it, that may be the point. To be honest, I suspect we all enjoy the detours more than the decisions, and my father, mind you, is usually the one who starts them.

titulo.es: La sobremesa: los cuatro recursos juntos

texto.es: En una sobremesa se combinan los recursos de la charla informal: ecos para reaccionar (Is she? Did he?), cabeza o cola para hablar de alguien (My sister, she's…; She's lovely, your sister), elipsis para acordar o rechazar (Neither can I, I'd love to, I'd rather not) y marcadores para dirigir el rumbo (By the way, Anyway, To be honest). Propón un tema, reacciona a lo que dicen los demás y cambia de tema con un marcador. Si solo hablas tú, no es una conversación.
Tema + reacción + cambio de tema:

formula.texto: “By the way, my sister, she's making the dessert.”

nota.es: marcador + cabeza: propones el tema

formula.texto: “Is she? I'd love to try it.”

nota.es: eco + elipsis: reaccionas al comentario
marcador: cambias o vuelves al plan

items.texto: “Please help yourself to more,” said the host. “Did you like the recipe? My grandmother would be thrilled to hear it.”

traduccion.es: «Por favor, sírvete más», dijo el anfitrión. «¿Te gustó la receta? A mi abuela le encantaría saberlo.»

nota.es: Help yourself invita a servirse sin ceremonias; la receta abre un tema fácil para la sobremesa.

items.texto: “I bet the boys will polish off that dessert before we reach the coffee.” “They will, won't they? They always do.”

traduccion.es: «Seguro que los chicos se terminan ese postre antes de llegar al café.» «Sí, ¿verdad? Siempre lo hacen.»

nota.es: Polish off significa terminar algo con rapidez; la tag won't they? pide compartir la opinión.

items.texto: “Have you heard the gossip about the neighbours?” “No. Go on, I'm all ears, and don't leave out the best part.”

traduccion.es: «¿Has oído el chisme sobre los vecinos?» «No. Sigue, soy todo oídos, y no te dejes la mejor parte.»

nota.es: Go on invita al otro a seguir; combina bien con un eco o con una petición de detalles.

items.texto: “I can't eat another bite.” “Neither can I. Shall we do the dishes now, or leave them until the morning?”

traduccion.es: «No puedo comer ni un bocado más.» «Yo tampoco. ¿Lavamos los platos ahora o los dejamos para la mañana?»

nota.es: Neither can I copia el auxiliar de can't; do the dishes es la colocación para lavar los platos.

items.texto: A running joke about the burnt toast, repeated every Christmas, is one way the host can steer the conversation back to lighter ground.

traduccion.es: Una broma recurrente sobre la tostada quemada, repetida cada Navidad, es una forma en que el anfitrión puede reconducir la conversación hacia temas más ligeros.

nota.es: Steer the conversation describe cambiar el rumbo con suavidad, por ejemplo con un chiste o un marcador.

items.texto: After the main course, Tom stood up to propose a toast to the host, and everybody laughed at his long introduction.

traduccion.es: Después del plato principal, Tom se puso de pie para proponer un brindis por el anfitrión, y todos se rieron de su larga introducción.

nota.es: Propose a toast es la colocación habitual; el brindis suele cerrar la sobremesa con humor.

texto.es: Contar (tell) nombra la emoción: She was nervous. Mostrar (show) da lo que el lector vería, oiría u olería, y le deja deducir la emoción: Her hands began to tremble; She bit her nails. texto.es: En la narrativa, el inglés altera el orden normal para dar ritmo. Anteposición de lugar: Down the hill ran the dog; si el sujeto es un nombre, el verbo va antes (ran the dog), pero con pronombre no hay inversión (Down the hill it ran). Un adverbio negativo al inicio pide auxiliar + sujeto: Never had she seen such a view. Los fragmentos sin verbo (Silence. Then footsteps.) crean tensión. Alterna frases largas con una corta que golpea. Si los usas en cada frase, pierden efecto.

titulo.es: Saltos en el tiempo de una anécdota

texto.es: Una anécdota casi nunca va en orden. La línea principal se cuenta en pasado simple (arrived, gave, talked). Lo anterior va en pasado perfecto (had promised, had told) y lo que ya duraba antes de un hecho, en pasado perfecto continuo (had been waiting). Lo posterior, visto desde el pasado, con would + verbo (she would marry him). Los marcadores ayudan: years earlier, by the time, three years later. Para reconstruir el orden real, ordena por tiempo verbal y marcadores, no por el orden en que aparece cada frase.

texto.es: Una anécdota con giro tiene tres partes. Escena: el fondo en pasado continuo con detalles (The rain was tapping on the windows). Hecho y giro: algo la rompe en pasado simple (Suddenly, a woman sat down), a menudo con una intención que no se cumple o una acción interrumpida: I was about to pay when… / I was going to call the police, but then… Desenlace: se anticipa con would, y tras little se invierte: Little did I know that she would become my partner. Sigue el orden escena → hecho → giro → desenlace.

items.audio: I was standing in the queue at the station café, tapping my foot, when I realised that my train was about to leave. I was going to run for it, but the man in front of me turned to face me and handed me his ticket. “I'm not going anywhere,” he said. Little did I know that he worked at the company where I had an interview the next day and, as luck would have it, he would be one of the people asking the questions.

consigna.es: Completa: «Yo no tenía ni idea de que el hombre del banco me cambiaría la vida.»

feedback.es: Little did I know es la fórmula fija que anuncia un giro; al inicio exige inversión con did.

feedback.es: Una buena anécdota abre con una escena en pasado continuo, la rompe con un hecho, usa was about to / was going to y anticipa el final con would (Little did I know…).

items.respuesta: It was a grey afternoon, and the rain was tapping on the windows of the library. I was about to return a book when I noticed a small note between the pages. Suddenly, my curiosity woke up. It was a phone number, and below it someone had written: “Call me if you find this.” I was going to throw the note away, but then I remembered how quiet the library could feel on a wet day, so I phoned. A woman answered at once. “Finally,” she said, laughing. “I left it there three years ago, as a joke.” We talked for an hour. Little did I know that she would become my business partner, and that we would open a small shop together. To my relief, the shop was an immediate success, and the note is still on the wall.

It was a rainy evening, and the wind was blowing hard outside the station. A few people were waiting quietly in the dark. I was about to get on the last bus when it dawned on me that my wallet was not in my bag. My heart was beating very fast. I was going to ask the driver for help, but a young woman handed me a ticket. “Don't worry,” she said. “Buy me a coffee one day.” I thanked her and sat by the window. Little did I know that I would meet her again. Two weeks later, she came into my new office, and she would become my best friend for the rest of my life, and my business partner too.

I was about to call out when I noticed a card sticking out of it: “If lost, please return to Mr Hall.” I handed it back and thought nothing more of it. Little did I know that Mr Hall owned the company where I had applied for a job. As luck would have it, he remembered my face on the day of the interview, and within a month I had signed my contract.

Every summer, the whole family used to meet at my grandmother's house. The kitchen smelled of coffee, and the relatives were all talking at once. My aunt Mia would always tell the same story about the day she lost her umbrella at the station. That year, she was about to start it again when a stranger walked into the garden, holding an old umbrella. Nobody recognised him. Silence. Then my aunt stood up and put her hand to her face. “It's mine,” she whispered. He had been looking for her for thirty years, and he had kept the umbrella in his house all that time. Little did we know that he would stay for dinner, and that he would become part of the family.
Did you recognise him? No, I didn't. I thought he was a neighbour.
What did your aunt say? Fair enough, she said. Tonight, for once, we will hear a new story.

Every year, at the family reunion, my uncle Carlos would tell the same story about the night he met my aunt. He would embellish it a little more each time, until the rain became a storm and the walk became a mountain climb. The distant relatives would smile politely, and my cousins would count the new details. Yet nobody ever stopped him. When he reached the punchline, the whole table burst out laughing, even those who could have told it word for word. Last year he forgot the ending. Nobody helped him. For once, we all just wanted to hear him find it.

Family stories are rarely accurate. Every retelling embellishes them, drops the awkward details and improves the punchline, until the tale says more about the family than about the event. Yet that, surely, is the point: nobody at a reunion wants a report; they want to hear themselves described, a little taller and a little funnier than they were.

titulo.es: Contar la anécdota en la reunión

texto.es: Contar una anécdota en una reunión junta todo lo aprendido. Abre con un hábito o una escena mostrada (At every reunion, my uncle would…; The kitchen smelled of coffee…). Rompe la escena con un hecho en past simple o con was about to; da el giro mirando hacia atrás (had been planning) y anticipa el final con Little did I know… + would. Cierra con una frase corta o un fragmento (Silence. Then laughter.). Después, responde al público con naturalidad: un eco, un marcador (Anyway, To be honest) y respuestas cortas.
Escena + hecho + giro + desenlace:

formula.texto: At every reunion, my uncle would tell…

nota.es: escena o hábito: would / used to

formula.texto: I was about to cut the cake when…

nota.es: hecho que la rompe, en past simple

formula.texto: Little did we know that… had been planning…

nota.es: giro mirando atrás y desenlace anticipado

filas.texto: Used to / would, past continuous, sentidos
I was about to cut the cake when…
Had been + -ing, Little did I know
…had been planning the prank for weeks.

items.texto: At every family reunion, my uncle would hold his audience with the same story, while the distant relatives pretended never to have heard it.

traduccion.es: En cada reunión familiar, mi tío tenía cautivo a su público con la misma historia, mientras los parientes lejanos fingían no haberla oído nunca.

nota.es: Would + verbo base abre la anécdota con un hábito del pasado; aquí una acción que se repetía.

items.texto: My grandmother had been planning for weeks to play a prank on the whole family, and nobody suspected a thing.

traduccion.es: Mi abuela llevaba semanas planeando gastarle una broma a toda la familia, y nadie sospechaba nada.

nota.es: Had been planning: una actividad en curso antes del momento que se cuenta; da el giro.

items.texto: Just as I was about to blow out the candles, the punchline of her joke arrived: the cake was made of bread.

traduccion.es: Justo cuando iba a soplar las velas, llegó el remate de su broma: el pastel estaba hecho de pan.

nota.es: Was about to + verbo se interrumpe con un hecho; el hecho que rompe la escena llega en past simple.

items.texto: Good storytellers tend to embellish, and it is easy to get carried away, so keep only the details that serve the story.

traduccion.es: Los buenos narradores tienden a adornar, y es fácil dejarse llevar, así que conserva solo los detalles que sirven a la historia.

nota.es: Embellish es adornar un relato; get carried away, pasarse de la raya por entusiasmo.

items.texto: If the prank were to backfire, the whole family would be ready to see the funny side, as they always were.

traduccion.es: Si la broma saliera mal, toda la familia estaría dispuesta a verle el lado gracioso, como siempre.

nota.es: If + were to + verbo base plantea una hipótesis poco probable; la familia reaccionaría con humor.

items.texto: When the story ended, the whole audience would burst out laughing, and someone always asked, “Did you really eat it all?”

traduccion.es: Cuando la historia terminaba, todo el público se echaba a reír, y alguien siempre preguntaba: «¿De verdad te lo comiste todo?»

nota.es: Las preguntas del público usan did + verbo base: Did you really eat…? Responde con una frase corta.

pista.es: Busca el past perfect continuous: lo que duraba antes del giro.

texto.es: En español también decimos «¡Qué bien!» cuando algo sale mal, pero el inglés lleva estos recursos más lejos. La ironía dice lo contrario de lo que se piensa; el understatement dice menos de lo que ocurre y quita importancia a un hecho grave, sobre todo en el inglés británico. Ninguno se anuncia: hay que comparar lo dicho con la situación. Si coinciden, la frase es literal; si chocan o se quedan cortas, hay intención. En un audio no ves la cara, así que el contexto es tu pista.

titulo.es: Juegos de palabras: una palabra, dos sentidos

texto.es: Un juego de palabras (pun) aprovecha que una palabra tiene dos sentidos (double meaning) o que suena igual que otra (homophone). Primero preparas un sentido y al final, en la punchline, aparece el segundo: todo el chiste depende de esa palabra clave (hinge on). No se traduce palabra por palabra, porque el chiste está en el inglés. Para explicarlo, localiza la palabra, di sus dos sentidos y muestra por qué encajan en la escena. Muchos puns provocan un quejido en vez de una carcajada, y eso forma parte del juego.
Preparación + palabra con dos sentidos + remate:

formula.texto: I used to be a banker,

nota.es: preparación: sugiere el mundo del dinero
giro: prepara el remate

items.audio: On the radio last week, a performer explained why he loves puns, even bad ones. A good pun, he said, is a small piece of engineering: the preparation builds one meaning, the punchline switches to another, and the audience has half a second to feel proud. Then comes the groan. He claimed that the groan is not an offence but the highest compliment, because it shows that the listener has understood and cannot forgive himself for enjoying it. Critics say that puns are the lowest form of humour. He smiled and said that they are, but that is exactly why people remember them.

consigna.es: Lee la carta al periódico: ¿qué critica en realidad quien la escribe?

feedback.es: El autor acepta el wordplay, pero rechaza que sustituya a la información: su objeción es al hábito, no a los juegos de palabras en sí.

opciones: The habit of using wordplay instead of informing readers.

items.texto: Your headline about the bank thief making a run for it might have made me smile if I had not read the same kind of pun three times this month. Headline writers seem to think that any word with two meanings deserves the front page. I do not object to wordplay; I object to wordplay that takes the place of information.

titulo.es: Sincero o sarcástico: busca las pistas

texto.es: El sarcasmo usa palabras positivas para criticar o burlarse («Thanks a lot!» cuando alguien te estropea algo). Tres pistas lo delatan: la voz (plana, alargada, con suspiro), el contexto (la situación contradice lo dicho) y el contraste entre palabras y gesto. Con audio sintético la voz no ayuda, así que fíjate en el contexto y en lo que se cuenta. Cuidado: so + adjetivo y such a + nombre intensifican tanto un elogio sincero como uno sarcástico: «You are so kind» puede ser verdad o burla.
Palabra positiva + pista + situación mala = sarcasmo:

nota.es: palabra positiva exagerada
pista de tono: suspiro o voz plana

In her column about public transport, the writer complains that her morning train is so crowded that she has learned to sleep standing up, that the train is such a tiny space that commuters exchange birthdays by the third stop, and that neither the conductor nor the timetable has ever told the truth. Readers love it, because nobody believes a word of it. The exaggeration is her way of saying that she is tired, and the jokes soften a complaint that might otherwise sound bitter. Her editor adds only one rule: never go too far, and never aim the joke at a person who could be hurt.
To turn the complaint into a joke so that it can be forgotten quickly.

To keep the mood friendly while still taking the complaint seriously.
To avoid offering a solution by making the whole matter a joke.

Dear Sara, I am sorry that your sandwich was cold. It was such a dramatic disaster that I have asked the kitchen to hold a minute of silence. Only joking: I have already arranged a free lunch for you, and I hope that this small gesture shows how seriously we take every complaint.

A quick smile and an “only joking” can ___ the edge off a sharp complaint. Without them, even a friendly exaggeration might sound like an attack.

My complaint is simple: the queue at the post office was so long that I learned to play the guitar while I waited. It was such a slow morning that the clocks went on strike, and both my patience and my shoes were worn out before I reached the window. Either the post office has forgotten how to count, or the staff are training to become statues. I am kind of upset, but I am only joking. My friend Leo answered at once: Poor you! You are so dramatic that the theatre should call you. Neither the queue nor the clerk deserves such an unfair review, but either you take a book next time, or I will bring you a chair. Only joking: come to my house, and I will make you a hot chocolate.

Escribe en inglés una queja exagerada sobre algo cotidiano (una cola, un atasco, un autobús) y la respuesta bromista de un amigo. Usa dos estructuras de intensidad (so… that y such a…), un correlativo (both… and, either… or o neither… nor) y un suavizador (kind of, only joking).
It is a form of lying that speakers should avoid.
It is acceptable in every situation, between any two people.
It is acceptable whenever the speaker says that he is only joking.
It is acceptable when both sides know that it is not literal.

I used to think that exaggeration was a form of lying. Now I see that it is a kind of contract: the speaker promises not to be taken literally, and the listener promises to laugh. The contract breaks only when the joke is about something that the other person cannot change, because then nobody is playing a game any more.

My brother sent me a complaint about the cinema. He said that the room was so cold that the ice cream froze, and that the film was so long that the credits felt like a holiday. titulo.es: Exagerar con gracia y sin herir

texto.es: La hipérbole exagera a propósito para hacer reír: nadie cree que la maleta pese un millón de kilos. Para intensificar usa so + adjetivo + that + resultado absurdo, o such a + adjetivo + nombre + that. Los correlativos reparten la queja: both… and (los dos), either… or (uno u otro), neither… nor (ninguno; el verbo va en afirmativo). Para no ofender, bromea sobre la situación o sobre ti mismo y añade un suavizador: kind of, sort of, I am only joking.

nota.es: such a + adjetivo + nombre

formula.texto: that I learned to play the guitar.

nota.es: that + resultado exagerado
correlativo: neither… nor con verbo afirmativo

formula.texto: I am only joking: we complained a lot!

nota.es: suavizador: avisa de que es una broma

feedback.es: La exageración expresa un cansancio real sin volver amarga la queja: los chistes la suavizan y la regla del editor limita el daño.

opciones: It hides her real opinion of the train behind jokes she does not mean.

items.audio: In her column about public transport, the writer complains that her morning train is so crowded that she has learned to sleep standing up, that the train is such a tiny space that commuters exchange birthdays by the third stop, and that neither the conductor nor the timetable has ever told the truth. Readers love it, because nobody believes a word of it. The exaggeration is her way of saying that she is tired, and the jokes soften a complaint that might otherwise sound bitter. Her editor adds only one rule: never go too far, and never aim the joke at a person who could be hurt.

consigna.es: ¿Qué busca con la broma del comienzo quien responde a Sara?

feedback.es: La broma exagera el problema para acercarse a Sara, y el almuerzo gratis y el cierre serio demuestran que la queja sí se toma en serio.

feedback.es: Take the edge off es la expresión fija para suavizar algo que resultaba demasiado duro.

items.texto: A quick smile and an “only joking” can ___ the edge off a sharp complaint. Without them, even a friendly exaggeration might sound like an attack.

consigna.es: Escribe una queja exagerada y la respuesta bromista de un amigo (180–240 palabras).

feedback.es: Una respuesta completa exagera con so… that y such a…, reparte la queja con un correlativo y mantiene el buen tono con un suavizador.

items.respuesta: My complaint is simple: the queue at the post office was so long that I learned to play the guitar while I waited. It was such a slow morning that the clocks went on strike, and both my patience and my shoes were worn out before I reached the window. Either the post office has forgotten how to count, or the staff are training to become statues. I am kind of upset, but I am only joking. My friend Leo answered at once: Poor you! You are so dramatic that the theatre should call you. Neither the queue nor the clerk deserves such an unfair review, but either you take a book next time, or I will bring you a chair. Only joking: come to my house, and I will make you a hot chocolate.

Come for dinner tonight, and I will cook pasta, so we can complain about the bus together.

He began well: he said that my cousin was so generous that he had once given away his only umbrella in a storm, and so late for everything that his own wife had learned to tell him the wedding started an hour earlier. Friends and family, please raise a glass to Mia, who turns thirty today! Mia is so generous that she cooks dinner for the whole street, and she is so late for everything that she arrived at her own party after the cake. I am only joking: we would wait for her all night. She is kind of famous for her terrible maps, but she is such a good friend that we always follow her anyway. I had planned a joke about her age, but I have decided to cut it, because it could be embarrassing for her and it would not be fair. Instead, I want to say something sincere: thank you, Mia, for being the first person to call when things go wrong, and the last one to leave when they go right. We are lucky to have you. Cheers, Mia, and happy birthday!

texto.es: Un buen brindis mezcla cariño y humor. Receta: (1) una o dos bromas amables sobre un rasgo inocente (llega tarde, cocina para todos), nunca sobre la edad, el aspecto, el dinero o algo que avergüence; (2) una hipérbole con so/such… that; (3) un suavizador si hace falta (kind of, I am only joking); (4) un cierre sincero con cheers. Antes de leerlo, revísalo: si un comentario puede ofender, quítalo o suavízalo (tone down).

An indirect refusal such as “I am afraid that might be difficult” spares the listener's feelings, but it rarely opens a negotiation.

texto.es: En muchos contextos del inglés, sobre todo el británico y el profesional, se evita el «no» directo. Se usan frases amables que funcionan como rechazo o desacuerdo: «That might be difficult», «I will think about it», «We must have lunch sometime», «With respect…». Las pistas: modales de duda (might, could), minimizadores (a bit, slightly) y la ausencia de fecha o alternativa. No es falsedad, es cortesía; en español un «no puedo» directo suele ser más aceptable. Es una tendencia: el contexto manda.

A researcher interviewed on a podcast recently described what she calls the airport effect. A traveller spends two hours in a foreign airport, meets three tired officials and decides that the whole country is unfriendly. The mistake, she says, is not in noticing a pattern, but in announcing it as a law. By and large, she added, people tend to be helpful when they are not exhausted. If you must generalise, leave room for the exceptions, because the exceptions are usually the people who change your mind. Her listeners laughed, but many wrote in afterwards to say that they had been guilty of the airport effect themselves.

texto.es: Las afirmaciones absolutas («All people here are rude») casi nunca son ciertas y pueden ofender. Para generalizar con cuidado el inglés ofrece: tend to + verbo base («People tend to be punctual»); marcadores de «en general» al inicio (by and large, as a rule, on the whole); it is not unusual for + sujeto + to + verbo; y cuantificadores como many, most o some en lugar de all. Diferencia con el español: para «soler» el inglés no tiene un verbo idéntico; se usa tend to o usually (y used to, solo para hábitos del pasado), y tend to va seguido de un verbo base.

nota.es: marcador: «en general»
sujeto: un grupo, no «todos»
tendencia: «suelen»; con sujeto plural, sin -s

When visitors first come to my house, they usually notice three things: the shoes by the door, the very long goodbye and the fact that my mother will not let anyone help in the kitchen. At first glance these habits may strike them as strange. By and large, however, they leave understanding that each one is a gesture of welcome: the shoes keep the floor clean for the children, the long goodbye shows that nobody is in a hurry, and the empty kitchen is my mother's way of saying that a guest is a guest. In my family, Friday dinner is a long-standing tradition. By and large, everybody is home by seven, and the children tend to choose the menu. For example, last week my little brother asked for rice and chicken, and we all agreed. A visitor is always welcome, and guests usually bring a dessert or a small gift. It is customary to share one big dish from the centre of the table, which may strike a visitor as unusual at first. In many countries each person has a separate plate, whereas in mine we pass the food around and talk while we eat. Neither way is better; each custom makes sense at home. Please do not worry if you are unsure what to do: my mother will show you, and she will give you a warm welcome. I hope that you can join us one Friday.

items.audio: My grandmother has a custom that surprises every visitor: before anyone eats, she puts a little food on a small plate by the window. She says it is a gesture of hospitality for anyone who might be passing. Whereas my cousins find it odd, I find it moving, because it reminds me that a welcome does not end at the front door.

items.audio: When visitors first come to my house, they usually notice three things: the shoes by the door, the very long goodbye and the fact that my mother will not let anyone help in the kitchen. At first glance these habits may strike them as strange. By and large, however, they leave understanding that each one is a gesture of welcome: the shoes keep the floor clean for the children, the long goodbye shows that nobody is in a hurry, and the empty kitchen is my mother's way of saying that a guest is a guest. Whereas in my friend's home everybody cooks together, in ours the cook is the host. Neither way is better; both are ways of saying: you matter.

items.respuesta: In my family, Friday dinner is a long-standing tradition. By and large, everybody is home by seven, and the children tend to choose the menu. For example, last week my little brother asked for rice and chicken, and we all agreed. A visitor is always welcome, and guests usually bring a dessert or a small gift. It is customary to share one big dish from the centre of the table, which may strike a visitor as unusual at first. In many countries each person has a separate plate, whereas in mine we pass the food around and talk while we eat. Neither way is better; each custom makes sense at home. Please do not worry if you are unsure what to do: my mother will show you, and she will give you a warm welcome. I hope that you can join us one Friday.

Please do not worry if you are unsure what to do: my mother will show you, and she will give you a warm welcome. I hope that you can join us one Friday.

Every Sunday my family has lunch at my grandmother's house, a custom that is older than I am. As a rule, everybody arrives around noon, and the younger cousins tend to arrive last. For instance, last month my uncle brought a cake that he had baked himself, and we all laughed because it was still warm. Visitors are welcome too, and they usually sit next to my grandmother. In some countries people eat quickly and leave, whereas in mine the table is a place to stay and talk for hours. Neither way is wrong; each custom simply suits its own home. It may seem unusual at first, but guests quickly feel at ease. I would love to see you there one Sunday.

When Jamal, an exchange student from Kenya, came to stay with us, my mother gave him a list of house rules, which was the first mistake. The second was my father's joke that only tourists ask for a second blanket. Jamal smiled politely, but the next morning he looked tired. My mother, who reads faces well, took me aside and suggested that we apologise for the joke, clarify that the list was not an order, and offer a blanket without comment. At breakfast my father said, with a smile, that he had been a bad host and a worse performer. Jamal laughed, accepted the blanket, and asked whether the house rules included the recipe for my mother's bread.

Dear Hana, you asked whether all the families in our town are as quiet as mine. It is a good question, and I should say first that I can only speak for the families I know. Many of them tend to be reserved at dinner, but others are noisy, particularly on Sundays. Please do not take our quiet as a sign that we are cold; it is simply how we were brought up.

Welcome, Carlos, and please feel at home! In my family we tend to eat dinner at six, and by and large everybody helps to set the table. Let me clarify something about last night: we did not mean to be rude when we started eating without you. I apologise, because I should have explained that we usually do not wait after seven. You asked a good question: why do we not talk more at dinner? It is a fair thing to wonder, and I will try to answer tactfully. Some families are quieter, and ours likes to enjoy the food first, whereas in your country people seem to talk more. Neither way is better, and it is only a habit; nobody is upset. Tomorrow we will talk as much as you like, and I will show you the city. No offence if we are quiet again on Sunday: my grandmother cooks, and we tend to listen to her stories.

explicacion.es: En español se concede algo a alguien, pero en inglés concede va directo con that + frase; no se añade you.

texto.es: En un debate bien construido el hablante primero reconoce un punto del otro lado (concesión): Admittedly…, I concede that…, I grant you that…, That is a valid point. Después da un giro con but, yet, even so, that said o nevertheless y defiende su postura (refutación). Al final cierra con To conclude… u On balance… Conceder no es rendirse: hace que tu refutación suene justa y segura. Al escuchar, busca la palabra de giro: lo anterior es la concesión y lo posterior es lo que el hablante realmente defiende.
Concesión + giro + refutación + conclusión:

nota.es: concesión: reconoces un punto del otro lado
giro y refutación: lo que realmente defiendes

formula.texto: To conclude, a ban is fairer.

items.texto: Admittedly, a phone is a lifeline in an emergency, but the office already has a landline for pupils.

items.texto: I concede that an outright ban is easy to explain, but its claim to raise results does not hold water.

traduccion.es: Reconozco que una prohibición total es fácil de explicar, pero su pretensión de mejorar los resultados no se sostiene.

nota.es: I concede that… cede un punto y but abre lo que se defiende. Hold water = resistir un examen: casi siempre se usa en negativa.

items.texto: Some pupils do use their phones sensibly; nevertheless, a single rule for everyone is easier to enforce and harder to dispute.

items.texto: To conclude, and on balance, I would keep phones in bags during lessons but allow them at break.

titulo.es: Por mucho que… y por muy… que…

texto.es: Además de although tienes estructuras concesivas más precisas y formales: Much as + sujeto + verbo («por mucho que»), However + adjetivo + sujeto + verbo («por muy… que»), adjetivo + as/though + sujeto + verbo («aunque sea…») y For all that + sujeto + verbo («a pesar de que»). En inglés no hay subjuntivo: el verbo va en presente o pasado normal. El adjetivo va delante, el sujeto antes del verbo (nada de inversión) y la segunda parte no lleva but.

texto.es: Para seguir un debate escuchado, busca cuatro piezas. La tesis (claim) es lo que el hablante defiende: My claim is… La evidencia son datos que se pueden comprobar: a survey, figures, According to… Una opinión («I think…») no es evidencia, y una sola anécdota tampoco es una muestra representativa. La objeción (objection) es el argumento contrario y la réplica (rebuttal) responde a ella. Recuerda que evidence es incontable: se dice the evidence shows, nunca evidences.
Tesis + evidencia + objeción + réplica:

nota.es: tesis: lo que defiendes
evidencia: dato comprobable
objeción: la postura contraria
réplica: respuesta a la objeción

texto.es: Para rebatir sin sonar agresivo, concede primero y luego combina tres recursos. Atenúa lo que no puedes probar con arguably, to a large degree o I have reservations about…; refuerza lo que sí sostienes con undoubtedly, clearly o by no means; y destaca lo importante con una frase hendida: What matters is… («lo que importa es…») o It is the cost that… («es el coste lo que…»). No mezcles atenuación y refuerzo en la misma afirmación, y recuerda que tras It is + elemento va that, no what.

items.audio: Carlos got up at the residents' meeting to answer Mia's proposal for a parking charge. He began by conceding that she had a reasonable point: the street really is crowded at weekends. Then he chose his words with care. The plan is arguably the simplest option, he said, but it is by no means the fairest, because it is the cost that families with two cars will overlook until the first bill arrives. He added that he had reservations about the timing, since a charge introduced in January would hit people who had just paid for the holidays. He never raised his voice. He simply repeated, calmly, that what matters is that nobody is priced out of their own street.

opciones: That some households would only discover the burden when the bills arrive.

items.respuesta: In my view, pupils should clean their own classroom once a week. Admittedly, it takes time away from lessons, and I have reservations about how often we can do it during exams. That is a reasonable point, but what matters is the habit we build: it is the pupils who use the room every day who should look after it, and it is undoubtedly fairer that everyone shares the work. Arguably, a clean room also helps us study, because nobody concentrates well among rubbish. Far from being a burden, ten minutes on Friday is a small price to pay. It is the cost of extra staff that the school would carry otherwise, and that money could buy books instead. To a large degree, the question is about respect, and what is essential is that we treat the classroom as ours. To conclude, a tidy room by no means needs a cleaner, only a rota.

I believe that pupils should clean their classroom every week. I concede that it takes time from lessons, and some parents think the school should do it. That is a valid point, but what counts is the habit we learn. It is the pupils who use the room all day, so it is undoubtedly fair that we look after it. Arguably, a clean room helps us study, because nobody concentrates well among rubbish. It is also the cost that the school would save, and that money could buy books for the library. Far from being unfair, ten minutes on Friday is a small price to pay. To a large degree this is a question of respect, and what is essential is that we share the work, because the classroom belongs to all of us. In conclusion, the whole class benefits, and nobody is asked to do more than a fair share.

Sol chaired the meeting about the old tennis courts. Mar spoke first and put forward her thesis: the courts should become a community garden. Her evidence was a petition with five hundred signatures. Tom, who has a vested interest because he trains there on Saturdays, conceded that a garden would look lovely, but what matters to him is that teenagers have a place to play. He proposed a compromise: half the land for vegetables, half for the courts. Mar did not accept at once. She said she would need to hear both sides of the club first, although she admitted that half a garden was better than none. Sol then put the idea to a vote.

As a resident, my position is that the park should stay open until ten at night. First, the petition has four hundred signatures, which shows that many neighbours want a say and want longer hours. Second, there is no other playground in this area, so families have nowhere else to go after work. Admittedly, there is some noise and rubbish after the weekend, and I have reservations about the late hours for the people who live next to the park. Much as I understand their tiredness, what matters is that children and parents have a safe place in the evening. It is the council that should clean the park and watch the noise, not the families who use it, and that should not come at the expense of the children. Arguably, closing at eight would solve one problem and create a bigger one. To conclude, we can reach a compromise: the park opens until ten, with a quiet rule after nine, and the council puts the plan to a vote.

titulo.es: Debate vecinal: todo el bloque junto

texto.es: En un debate vecinal encadenas lo aprendido en el bloque: tesis (My position is that…), dos argumentos con evidencia (First…, According to…), una concesión (Admittedly…, Much as I…) seguida de una refutación (nevertheless, what matters is…, it is… that…) y una conclusión con un acuerdo (To conclude, we can reach a compromise…). Declarar un interés personal y escuchar a ambas partes da credibilidad. Varía el tono con arguably y undoubtedly. Escucha primero qué concede el otro: así sabrás cuál es su verdadera objeción y podrás responderla con precisión.

nota.es: Put to a vote (voz pasiva) y hear both sides describen un proceso justo antes de decidir.

items.texto: To conclude, the council and the neighbours can reach a compromise: longer hours, a weekend cleaning team and quiet after nine.

nota.es: La conclusión cierra con un acuerdo concreto: reach a compromise = llegar a un término medio.

To conclude, we can reach a compromise: the park opens until ten, with a quiet rule after nine, and the council puts the plan to a vote.

explicacion.es: Para lamentar algo pasado el inglés exige had + participio; el español usa el pretérito y por eso se cuela explained.

texto.es: Salvar la cara (save face) es darle a otra persona una salida digna tras un error o un comentario brusco. En inglés se consigue quitando peso al error (It's easily done, No real harm done), asumiendo parte del problema (I may not have been clear, I'll take the blame) o suponiendo buena intención (I'm sure you didn't mean it that way; I'll give you the benefit of the doubt). Para lamentar algo propio del pasado usa wish / if only + had + participio: I wish I had explained it better. Nunca empieces por you always / you never.

titulo.es: Dejar la puerta abierta sin prometer

texto.es: Cuando no puedes o no quieres decir ni sí ni no todavía, el inglés cortés usa respuestas que no comprometen: I'll bear that in mind («lo tendré en cuenta»), Let me get back to you («ya te respondo»), I can't promise anything, It depends on…, I'd rather hold off at this stage. Dejan la puerta abierta sin mentir: no dices «sí», dices «aún no lo sé». Así mantienes la relación y ganas tiempo. Cuidado con la gramática: bear that in mind, depends on, y con can't promise el resto va en positivo: anything, no nothing.

texto.es: Los comunicados diplomáticos dicen cosas duras con palabras suaves. We note with concern equivale a «estamos preocupados y queremos que cambie»; a frank exchange of views, a «discutimos con dureza»; we regret, a «lamentamos lo ocurrido» (sin admitir culpa); we remain committed to…, a «seguimos dispuestos, pero no hay acuerdo». texto.es: Una queja suave tiene tres piezas. Primero describe el problema sin acusar: Lately, the kitchen has been a mess. Después expresa el deseo con wish + would (una conducta que molesta: I wish you would…) o if only + pasado (una situación: If only the walls were thicker). titulo.es: Mediar en la reunión del departamento

texto.es: Mediar es dirigir con tacto: dar turno, escuchar a todos hasta el final, resumir lo dicho y cerrar con un acuerdo. Combina lo visto en el bloque: la queja suave (I wish you would…, If only…), las peticiones y preguntas indirectas (I was wondering if…, Could I ask whether…?), las preguntas reportadas (Mia asked whether…) y las fórmulas para reconocer al otro y no comprometerse antes de tiempo. Antes de acordar, resume qué ha dicho cada uno; al final, cierra con una pregunta de acuerdo: Are we all happy with that?

texto.es: Los textos académicos prefieren sustantivos a verbos. When you evaluate a study, do not reach for the strongest word. Calling a study flawed because its sample is small is fair only if the authors claim more than that sample allows. A small study that says tentative things can be perfectly honest. Suppose two teams each test forty people. One team writes that the medicine always works; the other writes that the result is encouraging and deserves a larger trial. Their data may be the same, and yet only the first team has gone too far. The real fault is a claim that is bigger than its evidence.

texto.es: Para juzgar un estudio, el inglés académico usa adjetivos que dicen cuánta confianza merece. Robust y compelling valoran bien; flawed y questionable señalan debilidades; thorough elogia el cuidado del trabajo; tentative indica la cautela del autor y conclusive dice que la cuestión queda cerrada. Acompaña siempre el adjetivo con una razón (because, since o dos puntos) y, si quieres matizar, usa fórmulas como cast doubt on, lend weight to o fall short of. Un buen juicio es justo: distingue la calidad del método de la fuerza de la conclusión.

items.audio: When you evaluate a study, do not reach for the strongest word. Calling a study flawed because its sample is small is fair only if the authors claim more than that sample allows. A small study that says tentative things can be perfectly honest. Suppose two teams each test forty people. One team writes that the medicine always works; the other writes that the result is encouraging and deserves a larger trial. Their data may be the same, and yet only the first team has gone too far. The real fault is a claim that is bigger than its evidence.

Aim: This study examined whether phone use in lessons lowers exam results among adolescents. Method: We tracked 600 students in twelve schools for two terms; half of the schools banned phones in class. Results: Students in schools with a ban scored about four per cent higher, but the difference narrowed in the second term. Conclusion: The findings point to a small benefit, although we cannot rule out other explanations, and further research is needed.

Aim: This study examined whether later school start times improve the sleep and attention of adolescents. Method: We followed 240 students in four schools for one year; two schools moved the start of the day to nine o'clock, and two did not. Results: At the later schools, students slept about fifty minutes longer each night and reported better attention, although attention was self-reported. Conclusion: These findings point to a possible benefit. Because all four schools were in one city, we cannot rule out local factors, and further research is needed.

titulo.es: Leer un abstract: cuatro campos y una postura

texto.es: Un abstract resume un estudio en un orden fijo: objetivo (aim: qué se quería averiguar), método (quién, cuántos, cuánto tiempo), resultados (qué se encontró, con cifras) y conclusión (qué significa y qué límites tiene). La postura del autor se lee en el lenguaje: suggest, may o point to indican cautela; show, prove o will indican seguridad. Antes de sacar una inferencia, comprueba que va en consonancia con los datos y que no confunde coincidencia con causa. Lee primero el objetivo y la última frase: ahí están la idea central y hasta dónde se atreve a llegar el autor.

According to the council's study, the building of more than a hundred kilometres of new lanes for cyclists has been followed by a sharp growth in commuter cycling, from 3 to 11 per cent, and by a reduction in central traffic of nine per cent. Early opposition, especially from shopkeepers who feared losing customers to reduced parking, has proved wrong. The lead researcher argues that the scheme has already earned back its cost, since spending on road maintenance and health care has dropped, and she notes that shops beside the lanes now earn six per cent more. Some critics claim, however, that the findings for small firms cannot be trusted, because just forty of them replied. The researcher concedes that this is a weakness and recommends a second, larger survey next year, while the council, for its part, is considering further routes outside the centre but has not explained where the money will come from.

Five years ago, the city council decided to build more than one hundred kilometres of protected bike lanes. At first, many residents opposed the plan, and shop owners were especially worried, because they assumed that fewer parking places would mean fewer customers. However, the figures published this spring tell a different story. The proportion of people who cycle to work has risen from three per cent to eleven per cent, while car traffic in the centre has fallen by nine per cent. Air quality has improved, the main streets are quieter, and several schools report that more pupils now arrive by bicycle. The researcher who led the study argues that the investment has already paid for itself, because the city now spends less on road repairs and on health care. She points out that sales in the shops along the new lanes have grown by six per cent. Nevertheless, some critics claim that the results for small shops are unreliable, since only forty businesses answered the survey. The researcher acknowledges this limitation, and she suggests that the council should repeat the survey next year with a larger sample. Meanwhile, the council hopes to build more lanes in the north of the city, although it has not yet said who will pay for them.
That the council has lied on purpose about the survey results.

titulo.es: Parafrasear y atribuir: los verbos de cita

texto.es: Parafrasear es contar la idea de otra persona con tu propia estructura y tus palabras, y atribuirla siempre. El verbo de cita muestra cómo te sitúas: according to (con to) introduce una fuente neutral; argue, maintain y contend presentan una tesis defendida; claim toma distancia; acknowledge admite un límite; point out hace notar un dato. Tras el verbo va that + oración. Para condensar, usa nominalizaciones («cycling grew» pasa a «the growth in cycling») y no atribuyas dos veces: According to… y argue juntos sobran. Copiar textualmente sin comillas no es parafrasear.
Fuente + verbo de cita + that + idea condensada:

nota.es: fuente: quién lo dice (o bien According to the report, sin verbo de cita)

items.texto: To paraphrase a source, change the structure as well as the words, and keep the original meaning intact.

traduccion.es: Para parafrasear una fuente, cambia la estructura además de las palabras y conserva intacto el significado original.

nota.es: Cambiar dos o tres palabras no es parafrasear: hay que reorganizar la frase.

items.texto: Copying a sentence verbatim and changing two words is not paraphrasing; it is copying with a small disguise.

traduccion.es: Copiar una frase textualmente y cambiar dos palabras no es parafrasear; es copiar con un pequeño disfraz.

nota.es: Verbatim significa «palabra por palabra»; si copias así, debes citar con comillas.

items.texto: According to the survey, cycling has doubled: a reporting verb shows how far you agree with the source.

nota.es: According to (con to) introduce una fuente neutral; el verbo de cita añade tu actitud.

items.texto: Use claim to distance yourself from a statement that you doubt, and argue when you find the reasons persuasive.

traduccion.es: Usa claim para distanciarte de una afirmación de la que dudas, y argue cuando las razones te parezcan convincentes.

nota.es: Claim toma distancia; argue presenta una tesis defendida con razones.

nota.es: Maintain indica firmeza; contend es más formal, propio de textos académicos.

items.texto: A careful writer will point out a weakness, acknowledge a limit or take issue with a doubtful claim, without attributing anything twice.

traduccion.es: Un autor cuidadoso señalará una debilidad, reconocerá un límite o discrepará de una afirmación dudosa, sin atribuir nada dos veces.

nota.es: Cada verbo de cita expresa una función: señalar, admitir o discrepar; una sola atribución por idea.

consigna.es: Quieres dejar claro que dudas de lo que afirma la fuente. ¿Qué frase eliges?

feedback.es: Claim toma distancia de lo dicho; acknowledge admite que es verdad y maintain sugiere una convicción firme que tú no compartes.

pista.es: Busca el verbo que toma distancia de la afirmación.

Someone asked me whether exercise improves memory for everyone. Not quite. The study followed sixty adults, all of them volunteers, and the improvement was about eight per cent. It is thought that exercise helps, and the findings are in line with earlier work, but it is difficult to generalise from volunteers. On balance, the conclusion is tentative, with the proviso that older adults were not tested. I should add that this was a pilot study with a small sample, so it is thought that a larger trial would give a clearer picture, but nobody can say for certain until it is carried out.

The aim of this study was to examine whether taking notes by hand helps students remember more than typing. Briefly, one hundred and twenty students were followed for three weeks, and half of them wrote their notes by hand. Overall, the students who wrote by hand recalled six per cent more in a final test. It is widely assumed that handwriting is better for memory, and these findings are in line with that idea. It is worth noting that part of the difference may be attributed to motivation, since those students were all volunteers. To answer your question, we cannot say that handwriting is better for everyone, because all the participants came from one college, and it is difficult to generalise from a single group. On balance, the conclusion is tentative, and further research with students of different ages is needed before anyone gives firm advice to students.

titulo.es: Resumir un estudio: pasiva impersonal y cautela

texto.es: Al resumir un estudio para tu grupo, sigue el orden objetivo, método, resultado y límite. Briefly y overall ayudan a condensar, y on balance cierra con un juicio global. Para presentar ideas sin decir quién las sostiene, usa la pasiva impersonal: It is assumed / believed / thought that… o It has been shown that…, con el sujeto it obligatorio (en español basta «se piensa que»). Cuando alguien pregunte si el resultado vale para todos, responde con prudencia: It is difficult to generalise… y una conclusión provisional, con la salvedad que corresponda.

items.respuesta: The aim of this study was to examine whether taking notes by hand helps students remember more than typing. Briefly, one hundred and twenty students were followed for three weeks, and half of them wrote their notes by hand. Overall, the students who wrote by hand recalled six per cent more in a final test. It is widely assumed that handwriting is better for memory, and these findings are in line with that idea. It is worth noting that part of the difference may be attributed to motivation, since those students were all volunteers. To answer your question, we cannot say that handwriting is better for everyone, because all the participants came from one college, and it is difficult to generalise from a single group. On balance, the conclusion is tentative, and further research with students of different ages is needed before anyone gives firm advice to students.

titulo.es: Un plan de negocio: secciones y su lenguaje

texto.es: Un plan de negocio tiene secciones fijas y cada una usa su propio lenguaje. El resumen ejecutivo dice qué harás y para quién; el mercado describe el mercado objetivo y a los competidores; el marketing explica cómo te darás a conocer (will + verbo); las operaciones dan horarios y turnos; las finanzas indican cuánto dinero necesitas, el flujo de caja y cuándo llegarás al punto de equilibrio; los riesgos nombran lo que puede salir mal, con may; y el equipo muestra la experiencia de quienes lo harán. Para reconocer una sección, fíjate en las palabras clave y en el tiempo verbal.

texto.es: El vocabulario de un pitch es preciso y suele ir con una cifra o una razón. Scope es el alcance de un proyecto; stake, la participación que alguien tiene en el negocio; leverage (verbo), sacar partido de algo que ya tienes, como contactos o una marca; margin, la diferencia entre lo que cobras y lo que cuesta; overheads, los gastos fijos; niche, un espacio de mercado pequeño y concreto; viable, que funciona en la práctica; y scale up, ampliar el negocio. Gain traction y a foothold in describen los primeros pasos; economies of scale, el ahorro que llega al crecer. Usa cada término con un dato que lo concrete.

texto.es: Un plan de contingencia dice qué harás si algo sale mal. En registro formal se sustituye if por la inversión Should + sujeto + verbo base: Should demand fall, we will… (= If demand falls…). Otras fórmulas son in the event of + sustantivo y in the event that + oración. Failing that introduce el plan B cuando lo primero no funciona, y fall back on, draw on o as a last resort matizan el orden de las opciones. La consecuencia debe ser una acción concreta con will (o would si es muy hipotética); piensa también en el efecto en cadena de cada riesgo.

titulo.es: Calendario de proyecto: plazos, acciones en curso y encargos

texto.es: Un calendario de proyecto combina tres recursos. Para los plazos, by + futuro perfecto (will have + participio): By the end of March, we will have signed the lease (estará hecho antes de esa fecha). Para acciones en curso, futuro continuo (will be + -ing): This time next month, we will be painting the walls. Para tareas delegadas, have / get + objeto + participio: Leo is having the sign made (lo hace otra persona). Añade el estado del proyecto con on track, behind schedule o push back, y sitúa cada hito frente a un plazo improrrogable. Empieza cada frase por el plazo o el momento y di quién hace qué.

titulo.es: Presentar un plan y responder a objeciones

texto.es: Presentar un plan es un desempeño con orden fijo: apertura (saluda y di qué vas a mostrar), calendario (by + will have, will be + -ing), tareas delegadas (have / get + objeto + participio), un riesgo con su contingencia (Should… / In the event of…) y respuesta a las objeciones. Ante una objeción, reconoce la preocupación (I take your point), tranquiliza (let me reassure you) y respalda con un dato (back up). Mantén un tono realista: promete lo que puedes cumplir, mantén tus cifras (stand by) y usa may o expect para lo incierto.

titulo.es: Desconfiar del narrador y deducir el pasado

texto.es: Un narrador poco fiable cuenta la historia de un modo que no puedes aceptar sin más: se equivoca, exagera, oculta algo o solo ve una parte. Las pistas son detalles que chocan con su versión: un objeto, una fecha, la reacción de otro personaje. Para reconstruir lo ocurrido usa modal + have + participio: must have (casi seguro que pasó), can't have (casi seguro que no pasó) y might o could have (posible). En español dirías «debió de» o «no pudo»; en inglés la negación de la deducción es can't, nunca mustn't.

titulo.es: Motivo, símbolo y tema en una reseña crítica

texto.es: Al analizar una obra distingue varios niveles. El motivo (motif) es un elemento que se repite; el símbolo (symbol) representa una idea; el tema (theme) es la idea general que sostiene la obra; el presagio (foreshadowing) anticipa lo que vendrá. Para valorar el efecto usa verbos como evoke, convey o resonate with, y para el estilo, adjetivos como subtle o heavy-handed. Con allude to mencionas algo de pasada, y open to interpretation indica que el final admite varias lecturas.

titulo.es: Leer un relato con cinco preguntas

texto.es: Para comprender un fragmento hazte cinco preguntas. ¿Quién cuenta la historia y qué ve? Es el punto de vista. ¿Qué quiere de verdad el personaje? Es su motivación de fondo, que rara vez se dice. ¿Cómo suena el texto? Es el tono: distante, amargo, irónico. ¿De qué trata en el fondo? Es el tema. ¿Qué no se dice, pero se adivina? Eso se infiere. Responde siempre con una prueba: The tone is bitter, because… / We can infer that…, because…

I told her I was very happy for her. She sounded pleased with herself, the way people do when a long argument is over. Then I put down the phone, went into the hall and looked for a long time at the empty space where the piano had been. Behind it, twenty years ago, I had hidden my first real diary. Sensible, I said aloud, to nobody. Very sensible.

I would argue that the ending of The Blue Door is ambiguous on purpose. The narrator says that nobody ever lived in the house, but he can't have been honest, because he also says that his sister left after an argument. The wet letter is a clue: she must have been upset when she wrote it, and he might have kept it hidden for years. A plausible reading is that the blue door is a symbol of a memory that he cannot close. Carlos argues that the narrator is simply lying to us, and I concede that this is possible. However, I take issue with the idea that one lie spoils the whole book, and I am not entirely convinced that the writer wants us to be certain. But we should not read too much into one lie. The imagery of cold and rain makes the sadness resonate, and the ending stays open to interpretation. We will have to agree to disagree, Carlos.

texto.es: En un club de lectura no hay una única respuesta correcta. Propón tu lectura con prudencia (I would argue that…, A plausible reading is…), defiéndela con dos deducciones apoyadas en pistas (must have, can't have, might have) y reconoce lo que el otro acierte (I concede that…, You make a fair point). items.respuesta: I would argue that the ending of The Blue Door is ambiguous on purpose. The narrator says that nobody ever lived in the house, but he can't have been honest, because he also says that his sister left after an argument. The wet letter is a clue: she must have been upset when she wrote it, and he might have kept it hidden for years. A plausible reading is that the blue door is a symbol of a memory that he cannot close. Carlos argues that the narrator is simply lying to us, and I concede that this is possible. However, I take issue with the idea that one lie spoils the whole book, and I am not entirely convinced that the writer wants us to be certain. But we should not read too much into one lie. The imagery of cold and rain makes the sadness resonate, and the ending stays open to interpretation. We will have to agree to disagree, Carlos.

titulo.es: Jerga: qué significa y dónde se puede decir

texto.es: La jerga (slang) es vocabulario muy informal de amigos, series y redes. Para reconocerla hazte dos preguntas: ¿qué significa en registro neutro? (I'm knackered = I am exhausted) y ¿dónde se puede decir? Con amigos, sí; en una entrevista, con un cliente o en un correo formal, no, porque podrías dar la impresión de ser descuidado (come across as careless). Además, parte de la jerga es regional: knackered, gutted y chuffed son muy británicos; beat y awesome, más estadounidenses. Reconocerla ayuda a entender; usarla solo cuando toca evita que suenes descortés.

texto.es: Los hablantes nativos no construyen cada frase desde cero: usan bloques fijos que dan tiempo para pensar y muestran su actitud. The thing is… presenta un problema, To be fair… concede algo, Mind you… añade un matiz, Come to think of it… recuerda algo de repente, For what it's worth… ofrece una opinión con modestia y To cut a long story short… resume. Después del bloque, la gramática sigue siendo normal: forget, remember y stop cambian de significado según lleven to + verbo (algo pendiente) o gerundio (algo ya hecho o que se deja de hacer).
Bloque + idea con to o -ing:

nota.es: abre el problema; después va una frase completa
forget + to + verbo: no llamé
concede algo a favor del otro antes de criticar
stop + gerundio: dejó de contestar

filas.texto: To be honest, I'm not sure.

items.texto: Apparently, the landlord is selling the building; the thing is, nobody has told the tenants anything yet.

traduccion.es: Por lo visto, el casero vende el edificio; la cuestión es que nadie les ha dicho nada a los inquilinos todavía.

nota.es: Apparently cuenta lo que has oído; the thing is presenta el problema y va seguido de una frase completa.

items.texto: Basically, she forgot to book the venue; to be fair, nobody reminded her, and to be honest, I forgot too.

traduccion.es: Básicamente, olvidó reservar el local; siendo justos, nadie se lo recordó, y para ser sincero, yo también me olvidé.

nota.es: Forget + to + verbo: no hacer algo pendiente. To be fair concede; to be honest admite.

items.texto: Anyway, it's not like I mind helping, but come to think of it, I spent all of last weekend moving boxes.

traduccion.es: En fin, no es que me importe ayudar, pero ahora que lo pienso, pasé todo el fin de semana pasado moviendo cajas.

nota.es: Mind + gerundio (mind helping). Come to think of it introduce una idea que se recuerda de repente.

items.texto: She stopped talking to me straight afterwards; mind you, she had apologised twice, as a matter of fact, so basically we are fine.

traduccion.es: Dejó de hablarme justo después; eso sí, se había disculpado dos veces, de hecho, así que básicamente estamos bien.

nota.es: Stop + gerundio = dejar de hacer algo; stop + to + verbo = pararse para hacerlo. As a matter of fact refuerza un dato.

items.texto: To cut a long story short, he apologised, and for what it's worth, I believed him; anyway, that is all in the past.

traduccion.es: Resumiendo, se disculpó, y por si sirve de algo, le creí; en fin, todo eso ya es pasado.

nota.es: To cut a long story short resume; for what it's worth ofrece una opinión con modestia.

items.texto: Basically, chunks buy you thinking time; use them sparingly, or you may sound vague rather than fluent.

traduccion.es: Básicamente, los bloques te dan tiempo para pensar; úsalos con moderación, o podrías sonar vago en lugar de fluido.

nota.es: Un bloque debe ayudar a hablar con claridad, no llenar silencios sin sentido.

consigna.es: Completa: «Siendo justos, ella intentó llamarte dos veces.»

feedback.es: To be fair concede un punto a favor de alguien antes de seguir.

pista.es: Adjetivo de «justo» dentro del bloque que concede algo.

items.texto: You are upset that your sister missed your party. Your brother says: To be ___, she did try to call you twice, and she was stuck at work.

consigna.es: ¿Qué bloque cierra mejor esta conversación?

feedback.es: Anyway corta el tema anterior y permite pasar a otra cosa; mind you y basically no sirven para despedirse.

pista.es: Busca el bloque que cierra o cambia de tema.

items.audio: I asked my brother whether he had called Gran on her birthday. Well, apparently, the thing is, his phone had no battery, and, to be fair, he was stuck on the motorway for three hours. Mind you, it was four o'clock when I asked him, and the birthday was yesterday. Come to think of it, he did say in March that he would remember to call her. Anyway, for what it's worth, he has now promised to drive over on Sunday. To cut a long story short, Gran has waited a whole day for that call, and I suspect she will be waiting on Sunday as well.

titulo.es: Deducir palabras nuevas en notas de voz

texto.es: En una nota de voz hablada con rapidez no puedes parar a buscar cada palabra. Busca la pista que rodea a la palabra desconocida: un contraste, un ejemplo, una consecuencia o incluso el tono de voz. Con esa pista, formula una hipótesis (I think X means… because…) y comprueba que encaja con el resto del mensaje. No necesitas entenderlo todo: basta con get the gist of it, es decir, captar la idea general, y make out lo que puedas del resto. Las contracciones y las muletillas del habla natural también son pistas, no ruido.
Palabra desconocida + pista + deducción:

nota.es: la palabra que no conoces

formula.texto: that two suitcases fill the floor,

nota.es: la pista: una consecuencia del contexto

formula.texto: so it must mean very small.

nota.es: tu deducción, con must o probably

I landed on Sunday night, and my first diary entry is mostly about the taxi driver who did not stop talking.
On Monday I could not figure out the bus timetable, so I asked a stranger to rephrase her directions twice.
By Wednesday I had managed to sort out my phone contract, which is the only good news in my diary so far.
Culture shock hit me on Thursday; my diary says I could not get the hang of tipping, and I felt like a child.
When a shop assistant speaks too fast, I ask her to rephrase, and somehow we muddle through.
A week after I landed, I have pretty much settled in, and I can finally catch up on sleep and write a happier diary.

Friday. It is the end of my first week, and I am writing this on the train, so forgive the handwriting. On Monday I could not even buy a ticket. Today I negotiated a flat deposit in two languages, well, one and a half. To be honest, I am chuffed, although I would never say so to my mother, because she would tell everybody. Mind you, on Wednesday night I was so homesick that I read my old messages twice. Anyway, I have pretty much settled in. The plan for tomorrow is simple: sleep until noon.

texto.es: Un buen diario ordena los hechos por días (On Monday…, By Wednesday…) y combina tres cosas: bloques naturales (figure out, sort out, get the hang of, settle in), expresiones coloquiales (to be honest, mind you, bummer) y una estrategia de comunicación (I asked her to rephrase it). Para llegar a 200–260 palabras, dedica dos o tres frases a cada día importante y cuenta cómo te sentiste, no solo qué hiciste.

titulo.es: Resolver un problema en inglés sin asentir a ciegas

texto.es: Esta clase reúne todo el bloque. Cuando tienes un problema en otro país: plantéalo con datos (The heating has not worked since Monday), pide una acción con cortesía y un plazo (Could you send someone to fix it by Friday at the latest?), y si la otra persona usa jerga que no entiendes, no asientas: repite la palabra y pregunta What do you mean by…? Después confirma con tus palabras (To make sure I understand, …). Para resumir tu semana usa bloques (To be honest…, The thing is…) y verbos con to o -ing (manage to, avoid + -ing).

texto.es: Una apertura eficaz hace dos cosas seguidas: primero capta la atención con un gancho y luego orienta al público con una señal de organización. El gancho puede ser una anécdota, un dato, una promesa o una pregunta, y cada uno produce un efecto distinto: la anécdota conecta, el dato sorprende, la promesa compromete. Al escuchar, pregúntate con qué abre el orador, qué efecto busca y qué señal anuncia la estructura. No basta con clasificar: justifica tu respuesta con las palabras exactas del orador.

texto.es: Las señales de organización guían al público por la charla: First abre la serie, Moreover suma un punto, Having said that matiza lo anterior, Moving on cambia de sección y To sum up anuncia el cierre. La pregunta retórica (Who has never…?) no espera respuesta: invita a pensar y a reconocerse en lo que se dice. Úsala tras un dato o una afirmación y deja una pausa breve. Cuidado con dos trampas: acumular señales que dicen lo mismo y preguntar tantas veces que el público deje de escuchar.

Every morning, millions of us do the same thing. We turn on the tap, we wait for the water to warm up, and we let it run. Who has ever counted how many litres disappear in those two minutes? Nobody, I suspect. Never have we had so much clean water, yet rarely do we treat it with respect. Not only do we waste water at home, but we also waste the energy that heats it. Here is what I suggest: three simple habits. First, keep a bowl in the shower. Second, turn off the tap while you brush your teeth. Third, repair every leak this week. Little did I know that three small habits would cut our bill by a third. Under no circumstances should we wait for a crisis, because water that has gone cannot be replaced. So tomorrow morning, turn off the tap, hold the bowl and feel what a difference it makes.

Tema: el agua en casa. Escribe en inglés el centro de una charla (150–230 palabras): incluye al menos una inversión enfática (Never have we…, Rarely do we…, Not only do we… but…, Little did I know…), una regla de tres (anuncia «three habits», «three rules»… y enuméralas) y una pregunta retórica.

Not until I stood beside the dry river behind my grandfather's house did I understand what a bad summer means. Seldom had I seen him so quiet. Then he picked up some dust and let it fall through his hands, and little did I know that this silent moment would shape everything I do today. My grandfather never gave a speech in his life, yet that afternoon he taught me more than any lecture. Rarely do we connect a number on a bill with an empty river, but at no point should we separate them.
That we should always link what we use at home to its effect on nature.

That anyone who checks a bill closely will soon waste far less water.

Critical: too many examples make a speech feel like a performance.
Neutral: the effect depends on how well the audience knows the speaker.

texto.es: La inversión da énfasis: cuando una frase empieza con una expresión negativa o restrictiva (Never, Rarely, Seldom, Little did, Not until, No sooner, At no point, Under no circumstances), el auxiliar pasa delante del sujeto. Pasos: 1) coloca la expresión al inicio; 2) sube el auxiliar (do, have, did, should) antes del sujeto; 3) deja el verbo principal en base o participio. Si no hay auxiliar, añade do/does/did. No es una pregunta, sino un recurso de énfasis. Úsalo una o dos veces por discurso y combínalo con la regla de tres y la pregunta retórica.

items.respuesta: Every morning, millions of us do the same thing. We turn on the tap, we wait for the water to warm up, and we let it run. Who has ever counted how many litres disappear in those two minutes? Nobody, I suspect. Never have we had so much clean water, yet rarely do we treat it with respect. Not only do we waste water at home, but we also waste the energy that heats it. Here is what I suggest: three simple habits. First, keep a bowl in the shower. Second, turn off the tap while you brush your teeth. Third, repair every leak this week. Little did I know that three small habits would cut our bill by a third. Under no circumstances should we wait for a crisis, because water that has gone cannot be replaced. So tomorrow morning, turn off the tap, hold the bowl and feel what a difference it makes.
aceptadas: Every morning, millions of us do the same thing. We turn on the tap, we wait for the water to warm up, and we let it run. Who has ever counted how many litres disappear in those two minutes? Nobody, I suspect. Never have we had so much clean water, yet rarely do we treat it with respect. Not only do we waste water at home, but we also waste the energy that heats it. Here is what I suggest: three simple habits. First, keep a bowl in the shower. Second, turn off the tap while you brush your teeth. Third, repair every leak this week. Little did I know that three small habits would cut our bill by a third. Under no circumstances should we wait for a crisis, because water that has gone cannot be replaced. So tomorrow morning, turn off the tap, hold the bowl and feel what a difference it makes.

Think about the last time you left a tap running. Why did you do it? Because nobody ever told you that it matters. Seldom have we been asked to think about water, and rarely do we wonder where it goes. Not until a dry summer arrives do most of us notice. So let me give you three rules that cost nothing. First, take shorter showers. Second, use the washing machine only when it is full. Third, fix every leak at once. Little did my neighbours believe that these three rules could save a thousand litres a month, yet that is exactly what happened on our street. At no point should we say that one person cannot make a difference, because every street is made of people like you and me. So when you go home tonight, look at your tap, and ask yourself one thing: what will I change first?

items.audio: Not until I stood beside the dry river behind my grandfather's house did I understand what a bad summer means. Seldom had I seen him so quiet. Then he picked up some dust and let it fall through his hands, and little did I know that this silent moment would shape everything I do today. My grandfather never gave a speech in his life, yet that afternoon he taught me more than any lecture. Rarely do we connect a number on a bill with an empty river, but at no point should we separate them.

Quick question: how many of you have ever lost a tennis match to a ten-year-old? I have, and it changed my life. Three years ago, I was a beginner at our neighbourhood tennis club, and I wanted to quit after one week. Today I will tell you why I stayed. First, tennis taught me patience: I learned to wait before I move. Moreover, the club gave me friends who explained every mistake without laughing. Having said that, nobody ever made me feel small. titulo.es: Una charla breve, de principio a fin

texto.es: Una charla de cinco minutos reúne todo el bloque: abre con un gancho (pregunta, anécdota, dato o promesa), anuncia tres ideas con señales (First, Moreover, Having said that), añade una inversión o una regla de tres para el énfasis y cierra con un takeaway que retoma el inicio. Después llega la pregunta del público: agradece, responde breve y vuelve a tu mensaje. Antes del día, ensaya en voz alta con un cronómetro: si te pasas de tiempo, recorta ejemplos en lugar de hablar más deprisa.

Did you know that nine out of ten people who start a book club give up before the third meeting? I almost did. Last year I was a beginner, too shy to speak, and I told myself that nobody wanted my opinion. Today I will show you how I changed my mind. First, I chose a book that I loved, because passion is easier to share than duty. Moreover, I wrote down one question before every meeting. Second, I listened, and having said that, I also learned to disagree politely. Not only did the club improve my reading, but it also gave me the courage to speak in front of strangers. Third, I kept going even when the book was difficult. In conclusion, choose well, prepare one question and stay for the whole evening. That is my message. Good question, by the way: you asked whether you must be a fast reader to join. Not at all; slow readers often say the most interesting things.
