texto.es: En una mesa redonda cada frase cumple una función de turno. Tomar la palabra: If I may… / Can I chime in here? Mantenerla: As I was saying… / Let me finish. Interrumpir: Sorry to interrupt, but… Ceder el turno: I will hand over to… / Go ahead… / Over to you. Al escuchar, fíjate en el verbo y en quién habla: el moderador da y cede turnos; los participantes los piden, los mantienen o, si no lo hacen bien, hablan encima del otro. La cortesía se nota en la disculpa breve y en el modal (may, could).

texto.es: Tres funciones, tres fórmulas corteses. Interrumpir: Sorry to cut in, but… / If I could just… Pedir aclaración: Can I just check…? / Could you pin down…? / To put it another way… Reconducir: Coming back to… / Is that directly relevant to…? La cortesía sale de una disculpa breve, un modal suave (could, might) y un propósito claro. Tras can o could el verbo va en base, sin to, y cut in no lleva complemento directo. Si te corrigen, responde con take that on board en lugar de justificarte.

Sara, who was leading the panel, waited for a pause and said: Sorry to cut in, Leo, but is this directly relevant to our budget? Leo laughed and admitted that he had gone off on a tangent. Sara thanked him and continued: Coming back to the budget, could you pin down how much a class set of tablets would cost? items.texto: Many panel moderators fear the word no. They let a guest drift from the subject because stopping him feels rude. I think the opposite is true. A polite way to redirect the talk, such as coming back to our question, protects the speaker who is being ignored, the audience who came for the topic, and, in the end, the guest who drifted, who would rather be stopped gently than be remembered for rambling.

titulo.es: Resumir lo que dijeron los demás

texto.es: Para resumir una mesa redonda, sustituye said por verbos que muestren la postura de cada persona: stressed (subrayó), doubted (dudó), insisted (insistió), warned (advirtió), suggested (sugirió), o concede a point y freely admit para una concesión. Elige el verbo por la intención, no por cortesía: doubted no es denied. Tras that, la frase suele retroceder un tiempo (can → could, will → would), salvo con modales como must. Al escuchar, pregúntate: ¿defiende, duda, avisa, concede o propone? Y no confundas a quien habla con la persona de la que hablan.

titulo.es: Construir sobre la idea de otro

texto.es: Un buen acuerdo parcial reconoce lo válido y después matiza: I take your point… / I agree up to a point, but… / That is a valid point; however… Luego amplías con Building on that… o Furthermore… y respaldas con For instance,… Por último, devuelves el turno con una pregunta dirigida a otro participante: Mia, what have you noticed? Así la mesa avanza en lugar de acumular opiniones sueltas. Recuerda: agree es un verbo, no un adjetivo, y partly va delante del verbo (I partly agree).

dialogo.texto: I take your point, Ana, and I agree up to a point, but I see one drawback: screens can distract.

traduccion.es: Entiendo lo que dices, Ana, y estoy de acuerdo hasta cierto punto, pero veo un inconveniente: las pantallas pueden distraer.

dialogo.texto: That is a valid point. For instance, my brother stops reading when a message arrives.

traduccion.es: Es un punto válido. Por ejemplo, mi hermano deja de leer cuando llega un mensaje.

dialogo.texto: Building on that, Ana, what do you do to avoid it?

traduccion.es: Partiendo de eso, Ana, ¿qué haces tú para evitarlo?

consigna.es: ¿Qué inconveniente señala Carlos?

feedback.es: Carlos concede parte de la idea de Ana y señala el inconveniente: «screens can distract».

opciones.es: Que las pantallas pueden distraer a los alumnos.
Que el papel resulta demasiado caro.
Que los alumnos no tienen tablets.

consigna.es: Escribe tu intervención: acuerdo parcial, ampliación con ejemplo y una pregunta.

feedback.es: Una buena intervención reconoce lo válido, matiza el acuerdo, amplía con un ejemplo y devuelve el turno con una pregunta a Mia.

items.respuesta: Thank you, Leo. I take your point, and I agree with you up to a point. Tablets are light, they are cheap to update, and a child can carry a whole library in one bag. But I see one drawback in a complete switch: many pupils read more slowly on a screen, and they get distracted by notifications. For instance, last month my teacher asked us to read a short story on a tablet, and half of the class ended up checking messages. Building on your idea, I would suggest a simple compromise: tablets for research and exercises, and paper for long reading. Furthermore, we could ask pupils to help us write the rules, because people follow what they choose. That is partly why I would not remove paper completely. Mia, what have you noticed with the younger children you work with? Do they read better on paper or on a screen? I would like to hear your view before we decide anything.

Mia, what have you noticed with the younger children you work with? Do they read better on paper or on a screen? I would like to hear your view before we decide anything.

Thanks, Leo. That is a fair point, and to a certain extent I agree with you, because tablets really do save a lot of weight and money. However, I see one problem: a screen makes it easy to open something else. For example, yesterday I tried to read a chapter on my tablet and I answered four messages before the end of the first page. Expanding on your idea, I would like to propose that every school keeps a set of paper books for long reading, and uses tablets for everything else. I would add that pupils should choose the books themselves, because a child reads more when the book belongs to them. Mia, what is your experience with the youngest pupils? Would the same plan work for them, or do they need something different? I am curious about your view, and I would like to hear it before we make any decision.

items.audio: Homework builds habits, and I agree with Leo up to a point. But for some pupils it only adds stress, and I have seen that with my own eyes. Take the case of my neighbour's son: he finishes his homework at ten at night and then cannot sleep. Furthermore, the teachers who set the most homework rarely have time to mark it properly, so the effort often disappears without a word of feedback. So I would not remove homework completely; I would reduce it, and I would make sure that every task counts for something.

consigna.es: Escucha de nuevo: ¿qué da a entender sobre los profesores que mandan más tareas?

feedback.es: Dice que rara vez tienen tiempo de corregirlos bien: sugiere que las tareas reciben menos atención de la debida.

opciones: That they may not give it the attention it deserves.
That they do not believe that it builds good habits.
That they are unaware of the stress that it causes.

Good evening, everyone, and welcome to tonight's panel. Our topic is technology in the classroom. Let me introduce our three panellists: Ana, who uses tablets every day; Tom, who teaches science; and Sara, who has three children at school. Ana, would you like to start? Thank you, Ana. Tom, it is your turn. Sorry to cut in, Tom, but coming back to the main question, could you pin down the cost? Thank you. Before we move on, let me draw the threads together. Ana stressed that tablets saved time. Tom doubted that schools could afford them, and he warned that screens could distract pupils. Sara suggested that we write clear rules, and she conceded that tablets had real benefits. Sara, what would your first rule be? Seldom have I seen three guests agree on so much. To wrap up, all of you agree that rules matter more than machines. I am deeply grateful to each panellist for a lively discussion, and I thank our audience for listening. Good night, everyone.

texto.es: Moderar es estructurar, no opinar. Empieza con una bienvenida y presenta el tema y a los ponentes (Let me introduce…), y fija el orden del día. Reparte los turnos con claridad (Ana, would you like to start? Tom, your turn) y, si alguien se desvía, reconduce con cortesía (Sorry to cut in, but coming back to…). Antes de cerrar, hila las ideas con verbos variados (Ana stressed…, Tom doubted…) y termina agradeciendo (To wrap up…; I am deeply grateful to…). Un buen moderador habla poco y deja que los ponentes se oigan entre sí.

vocabulario.texto: An interviewer rarely asks a question for its own sake; behind each one lies a quality the committee wants to gauge.
Tell me about a challenge you faced asks for evidence from the past, so a strong applicant answers with a real episode.
A hypothetical question may leave you feeling put on the spot, yet it tests your judgement rather than your record.
Questions about underlying motivation, such as what first drew you to this scholarship, invite personal reasons rather than a summary of the brochure.
When asked about a limitation, a candid applicant names a genuine weakness and explains how she is working to overcome it.
Could you elaborate on that? signals that your answer was too general and that the interviewer hopes to draw out more detail.
Talk me through a decision you came to regret.
How would you respond if your funding were cut mid-year?
What was it that first drew you to this scholarship?
Which of your skills would you say still falls short?
A promise that the applicant will avoid difficulty in future.
More detail about what the applicant actually found hardest.
A sign that the project was badly managed overall.
You described the project as a difficult year. Could you elaborate on that? I am interested in what exactly you found hardest, and what you would do differently now.
The interviewer said, “Suppose the funding were cut tomorrow. How would you respond?” It is a ___ question, because it tests judgement rather than experience.
She answers a question about motivation with a plan for overcoming her own weakness.
She answers a request for more detail with a general statement about herself.
She answers a question about motivation with facts anyone could find in the brochure.

Asked what first drew her to the scholarship, the applicant spent a full minute listing what the brochure says about the course: its staff, its buildings and its reputation. The committee chair listened politely, but it was clear that she had been hoping for something personal, a reason that only this applicant could give.
It is a hypothetical question; she answers it with a detailed story.
It is a motivation question; she avoids giving any real reason.
It is a leading question; she accepts its premise without any doubt.
It is a leading question; she concedes a point but keeps her view.
Interviewer: Surely you would agree that anyone serious about this scholarship would give up their weekends to study? Applicant: Well, I see the point, although I would say that rest matters too.

Skilled interviewers rarely rush. They use silence and short follow-up questions to draw ___ details that an applicant would not offer freely.
Is there a part of the role you feel unsure about?
Suppose two referees gave you opposite advice. What then?
Describe a time you disagreed with your boss.
What would keep you going when the work grows boring?
You mentioned a difficult year. Could you say more?
To see whether the candidate accepts a premise or politely challenges it.
To make the candidate feel relaxed before the harder questions begin.
To test whether the candidate has read the course description closely.
To hurry the candidate towards the answer she already expects to hear.

On this week's episode, a former scholarship officer explained what she really listens for. Candidates, she said, prepare for the questions they fear, such as the one about weaknesses, and then stumble over the ones that look simple. Where do you see yourself in five years? sounds like small talk, but it is her way of gauging whether an applicant's ambitions fit the course. She also admitted that she sometimes asks a leading question on purpose, simply to see whether a candidate will quietly agree or politely push back. Silence, she added, costs her nothing, and it often draws out the most honest answers.
That hypothetical questions should be dropped because candidates handle them too well.
That polished answers may hide how little some candidates reflect on themselves.
That the applicants have no real limitations worth mentioning to the committee.
That coaching is unfair and should be banned from future scholarship rounds.

Thanks for sitting in on Tuesday's interviews. I noticed that most applicants answered the hypothetical question fluently, yet very few could name a real limitation without rushing to a positive. That may say more about how they were coached than about their character, so I suggest we ask the second kind of question earlier next year.

items.audio: On this week's episode, a former scholarship officer explained what she really listens for. Candidates, she said, prepare for the questions they fear, such as the one about weaknesses, and then stumble over the ones that look simple. Where do you see yourself in five years? sounds like small talk, but it is her way of gauging whether an applicant's ambitions fit the course. She also admitted that she sometimes asks a leading question on purpose, simply to see whether a candidate will quietly agree or politely push back. Silence, she added, costs her nothing, and it often draws out the most honest answers.

texto.es: Las preguntas indirectas suenan más corteses y dejan hablar al otro. Tras Could you tell me…, I am curious… o I would like to know…, el orden es el de una frase afirmativa: sujeto + verbo, sin did ni inversión (why you chose). Para el sí/no usa whether o if. Las preguntas de sondeo directas, en cambio, sí llevan auxiliar: To what extent did…? What precisely do you mean by…? Sirven para pedir grado, exactitud o más detalle cuando la respuesta fue vaga. Combínalas: primero la cortés y, si hace falta, la de sondeo.

texto.es: Una respuesta fuerte tiene dos piezas: un ejemplo concreto (qué hiciste, cuándo y cómo) y un resultado que se pueda contar (cifras, plazos, efectos). Una respuesta vaga usa relleno (things, somehow, went well) o generalizaciones sin apoyo (I always…). Al escuchar, pregúntate dos cosas: ¿hay un ejemplo? ¿hay un resultado medible? Si falta una pieza, el entrevistador lo notará y pedirá: Could you be more specific? Con cifras de cambio usa by (fell by forty per cent) o from… to….

Last spring, I was in charge of the school recycling project, which had been struggling since the previous autumn.
When I arrived, the bins were overflowing because nobody had collected the paper for a week, and most students had stopped caring.

It was also a hard-won lesson about listening first: the project began to turn around only once each captain felt heard.

Two years ago, I was in charge of the school charity concert, which was already in trouble when I took it over. Nobody had booked the hall, the posters had not been printed, and several students had lost interest. I decided to take the initiative. First, I drew up a simple checklist and asked each class to choose a captain who would report to me every Friday. Then I phoned the music teacher, who found us a hall within two days. As a result, we sold every ticket in a week, and the concert has become a yearly tradition since then. The school has raised twice as much money as before. The experience taught me that a clear plan gives people confidence. It was also a hard-won lesson about asking for help early, because the project only began to turn around once I stopped trying to do everything myself. Since then, I have used the same approach in every team I have joined.

texto.es: Una respuesta de entrevista fuerte cuenta una historia con cuatro pasos. Termina con la lección, que debe ser algo que solo tú podrías haber aprendido: The experience taught me that… Controlar los tres tiempos evita que la historia se mezcle y demuestra dominio del inglés.

items.respuesta: Two years ago, I was in charge of the school charity concert, which was already in trouble when I took it over. Nobody had booked the hall, the posters had not been printed, and several students had lost interest. I decided to take the initiative. First, I drew up a simple checklist and asked each class to choose a captain who would report to me every Friday. Then I phoned the music teacher, who found us a hall within two days. As a result, we sold every ticket in a week, and the concert has become a yearly tradition since then. The school has raised twice as much money as before. The experience taught me that a clear plan gives people confidence. It was also a hard-won lesson about asking for help early, because the project only began to turn around once I stopped trying to do everything myself. Since then, I have used the same approach in every team I have joined.

Last year, I was in charge of the school garden. When I joined, nobody had watered the plants for a month, and most of the volunteers had already stopped coming. I decided to start again with a clear plan. I made a watering rota, I asked each class to choose a captain and I called the science teacher to ask for help. Within a week, the garden looked alive again. As a result, it has produced vegetables every summer since then, and the canteen has used them in its menu. The experience taught me that people help when they know exactly what they have to do. I also learned that asking for support early saves a lot of time. Today I use the same method whenever I start a new project.

items.audio: During a scholarship interview, a candidate was asked about a time when she had led a team. She began with the situation: last summer, she was in charge of a clean-up campaign on the beach, and by the time she arrived, the volunteers had already split into two groups that refused to work together. She listened to both, drew up a shared plan and gave each group its own captain. The campaign has collected more rubbish every year since then. Asked what she had learned, she answered that a leader's first job is to make sure everyone knows who is responsible for what.

titulo.es: Ser el invitado de un pódcast

texto.es: En un pódcast tu papel es el de invitado: abre con cortesía (Thanks for having me), responde con historias de tres pasos (situación, acción y resultado) y controla pasado simple, pasado perfecto y presente perfecto. Puedes discrepar con tacto (That is a fair point, although…) y devolver el turno con una pregunta de sondeo: If I may turn that around, to what extent…? Evita respuestas vagas: da ejemplos y cifras. Al final, cierra con una síntesis: To wrap up, if there is one key takeaway for the listeners…

titulo.es: Ganar tiempo sin perder el hilo

texto.es: Ante una pregunta inesperada no hace falta responder al instante: hay frases para ganar tiempo, y conviene elegir su registro. Las informales (Hang on, let me think; Hold on) van bien entre amigos. Las neutras (That's a tricky question; Let me see) sirven casi siempre. Las formales (Allow me a moment to consider that) se usan en entrevistas y reuniones. Off the top of my head y offhand avisan de que das un dato de memoria, sin comprobar. Elige según quién escucha, y no abuses: una pausa breve vale más que tres muletillas seguidas.

items.audio: On the show, a speaking coach described three ways to buy time and ranked them by register. Hang on, she said, works among friends but sounds curt in a formal meeting. That's a tricky question is neutral, and useful because it flatters the questioner while you think. Allow me a moment to consider that is the most formal, yet it carries a risk: if the pause that follows is too long, politeness turns into anxiety. Her advice was to combine two of them, naming the difficulty and then thinking out loud, because listeners forgive a pause far more easily than they forgive an empty reply.

objetivo.es: Identificar el punto, la razón, el ejemplo y el cierre en respuestas improvisadas, reconocer tangentes y decidir cuál de varias respuestas está mejor ordenada y por qué.

vocabulario.texto: point
reason
example
conclusion
a rambling answer
go off on a tangent
briefly

A well-built answer opens with the point, stated in one sentence: my point is that cities need more bike lanes.
The main reason should follow at once, because an opinion with no reason gives the listener nothing to weigh.
Then add an example, such as accidents falling in my neighbourhood after the new lane opened, to drive the point home.
Close with a conclusion that repeats your point in fresh words rather than introducing a brand-new idea.
If you go off on a tangent, admit it briefly and get to the point; a rambling answer makes listeners lose the thread.
To stay on track, name your point, reason, example and conclusion in your head and check each one as you speak.
My view is that a longer break would help.
The main reason is that students get tired.
To illustrate, last week half the class fell asleep.
In conclusion, a longer break is worth it.

titulo.es: Las cuatro partes de una respuesta improvisada

texto.es: Una respuesta improvisada ordenada tiene cuatro partes. Primero el punto: tu postura en una frase (My point is that…). Después la razón: por qué piensas así (The main reason is that…). Luego un ejemplo que la apoye (For example…). Por último el cierre, que repite el punto (In conclusion…). Al escuchar a otros, busca cada parte y fíjate en cuál falta: una respuesta con opinión, pero sin ejemplo, suena a lugar común. Si te desvías, reconócelo y vuelve: Sorry, I'm rambling; let me get to the point.
Punto + razón + ejemplo + cierre:

nota.es: punto: tu postura
razón: por qué
ejemplo: un caso concreto
cierre: repites el punto

texto.es: Un lector crítico clasifica cada enunciado antes de aceptarlo. Un hecho verificable puede comprobarse en un registro, una medición o un documento público. items.texto: Anything presented as a verifiable fact should pass a simple test: can an independent reader verify it in a public record?

traduccion.es: Todo lo que se presenta como un hecho comprobable debería superar una prueba sencilla: ¿puede un lector independiente verificarlo en un registro público?

nota.es: Verify es el verbo de la comprobación; un hecho se apoya en un registro, no en quien lo cuenta.

items.texto: The report says the minister allegedly accepted gifts, which remains an unsupported claim until someone produces hard evidence.

traduccion.es: El informe dice que el ministro supuestamente aceptó regalos, lo que sigue siendo una afirmación sin respaldo hasta que alguien presente pruebas sólidas.

nota.es: Allegedly avisa de que nadie ha demostrado lo que sigue; hard evidence es incontable.

items.texto: A witness who repeats what a neighbour said is offering hearsay, and an anonymous source who cannot be named deserves extra caution.

traduccion.es: Un testigo que repite lo que dijo un vecino ofrece rumores, y una fuente anónima que no puede nombrarse merece aún más cautela.

nota.es: Hearsay es incontable: no lleva artículo ni plural.

items.texto: Whether the new stadium is ugly is a matter of opinion, so no record or measurement could ever verify it.

traduccion.es: Que el nuevo estadio sea feo es cuestión de opinión, así que ningún registro ni medición podría verificarlo jamás.

nota.es: Un juicio de gusto no se comprueba: es a matter of opinion.

items.texto: An official statement that publishes its official figures is stronger than a rumour that allegedly comes from someone inside the ministry.

traduccion.es: Un comunicado oficial que publica sus cifras oficiales es más sólido que un rumor que supuestamente viene de alguien del ministerio.

nota.es: Official statement y official figures permiten que cualquiera compruebe el dato.

items.texto: A sensational headline tempts readers to accept the story at face value, yet a careful reader will verify the key detail before sharing it.

traduccion.es: Un titular sensacionalista tienta a los lectores a aceptar la noticia sin cuestionarla, pero un lector cuidadoso verificará el dato clave antes de compartirla.

nota.es: At face value = tal como se presenta, sin comprobarlo.

feedback.es: Solo la fecha y el coste figuran en un comunicado que cualquiera puede consultar; lo demás es un juicio de gusto y una suposición sobre otros.

pista.es: Busca el dato que cualquiera podría comprobar en un documento oficial.

dialogo.texto: A message in our class chat says the school will close on Friday, and everyone is sharing it.

traduccion.es: Un mensaje en el chat de la clase dice que el colegio cerrará el viernes, y todos lo están compartiendo.

dialogo.texto: Who wrote it? It sounds like hearsay to me, and there is no official statement.

traduccion.es: ¿Quién lo escribió? A mí me suena a rumor, y no hay ningún comunicado oficial.

dialogo.texto: It says an anonymous source in the office told a parent.

traduccion.es: Dice que una fuente anónima de la oficina se lo contó a un padre.

dialogo.texto: Then I will not take it at face value. I will verify it with the head teacher before I share anything.

traduccion.es: Entonces no me lo creeré sin más. Lo comprobaré con la directora antes de compartir nada.

traduccion.es: Buena idea. Un rumor no es un hecho solo porque mucha gente lo repita.

feedback.es: Leo dice que lo comprobará con la directora antes de compartir nada: no lo acepta sin más.

consigna.es: Escucha el pódcast y elige lo que la locutora da a entender sobre la noticia.

feedback.es: La locutora admite que el rumor podría ser cierto, pero critica que se presentara como hecho y se repitiera sin comprobar: así «a worry becomes a fact».

opciones: The plant will almost certainly close, whatever the company says in public.
The website invented its anonymous source to attract more readers.
Repeating an unverified headline can turn a rumour into accepted fact.
Companies should never comment on rumours about their own plans.
items.audio: Last week a local website ran a story under the headline Plant to Close, Hundreds to Lose Jobs. Within hours it had been shared thousands of times. I phoned the company, and a spokesperson told me that no decision had been taken and that an official statement would follow on Friday. The website's only source was an anonymous message posted by someone who claimed to work there. Of course, the rumour may turn out to be true. But the writer presented a possibility as a verifiable fact, and readers who took the headline at face value went on to repeat it. That, in my view, is how a worry becomes a fact.

feedback.es: Se dice que el municipio tiene pruebas de la bajada, pero no las ha publicado: es una afirmación sin respaldo. El porcentaje y la muestra son datos; «the best» es opinión.

When the city installed speed cameras on Harbour Road, serious accidents fell by a third in two years, and the council was quick to claim the credit. I am not so sure. Over the same period the road was repaired, a new bridge opened, and a petrol price rise kept many drivers at home. Each of these could be a contributing factor. titulo.es: Causa, correlación o posibilidad: tres niveles de certeza

texto.es: Al leer datos separa tres niveles. Causa probada: causes, leads to, gives rise to; exige un mecanismo (causation). Posibilidad: may, might o could + account for. La regla: no afirmes cause si solo tienes correlación; y recuerda que una correlación no implica necesariamente causalidad.

objetivo.es: Reconocer en publicaciones breves el falso dilema, la generalización apresurada, el ataque personal y el sesgo, y nombrar la debilidad con una razón.

Flawed reasoning often hides in a fallacy, a step that sounds convincing but collapses the moment someone examines it closely.
Either we ban phones completely or students will never concentrate: a false dilemma hides a weakness, because other options exist.
Two rude tourists are an unrepresentative sample, so it would be a hasty generalisation to assume that every visitor behaves the same way.
When a reply criticises the speaker's age instead of her argument, it is a personal attack, and the original weakness remains untouched.
To build a straw man, a writer distorts an opponent's view and then defeats the distortion, a fallacy that rewards careless listeners.
Survey bias appears when a writer decides to cherry-pick only the answers that support the conclusion, which produces a one-sided picture.
It is a hasty generalisation: it builds a rule from very few cases.
It is a false dilemma: it offers two options when others exist.
It is a personal attack: it criticises people instead of ideas.
Either we ban every phone in school or our results will keep falling. There is simply no other choice, and pretending otherwise only wastes everyone's time.

titulo.es: Falacias y sesgos: nombrar la debilidad y dar una razón

texto.es: Criticar un argumento no es decir «no me gusta»: es nombrar su debilidad y dar una razón. Un false dilemma ofrece solo dos opciones cuando hay más; una hasty generalisation convierte pocos casos en una regla; un personal attack critica a quien habla, no lo que dice; un straw man deforma la postura ajena. El bias y el cherry-pick afectan a los datos: se eligen las respuestas que convienen. Usa la fórmula nombre + because + razón, y evita assume sin pruebas.

Last term our school introduced a silent lunch hour, and the results are surprising. Complaints about noise fell by half, and teachers say that afternoon lessons are calmer. One teacher told me that pupils now return to class ready to work. Some students complained at first, but they soon adapted. I interviewed three of them, and all three admitted that they prefer the quiet. A parent also told me that her son comes home less tired and does his homework without any argument. So the policy is a success, and every school in the country should adopt it immediately, because silence is exactly what teenagers need.

The author of the post replied politely. She accepted that her sample was small, but insisted that the pattern was clear. The critic answered that a clear pattern in a small sample is exactly what chance produces, and asked whether she would repeat the survey with more classes. The author did not reply again.

The post makes an interesting point, but I think its conclusion needs more care. First, the writer seems to overlook the size of the sample: only thirty pupils from one class were asked, so the result may fall short of what a general claim requires. Second, the post rests on the idea that headphones stop fights, but it gives no evidence of how the fights were counted, which leaves the method open to question. To some extent, the fall in fights is likely to be linked to the headphones, although other factors, such as the weather or a new teacher, may also account for it. Arguably, the pupils who use headphones are simply the quiet ones, so the link is tenuous. Rather than handing out headphones in every school, a reasonable alternative would be to survey several classes for a whole term and compare the results. A balanced critique must also admit that the idea is worth testing, and I would certainly support a careful trial.

titulo.es: Criticar con matices: justificar, dudar y proponer

texto.es: Una crítica escrita eficaz no ataca: pondera. Organízala en cuatro movimientos. Dos críticas justificadas, cada una con su razón (The post seems to overlook…, because…; Arguably, the main weakness is…). Una relación o causa con duda (is likely to be linked to…, although other factors may matter). Una concesión (To some extent…). Y una alternativa razonable (rather than…, a reasonable alternative would be to…). Esos matices suavizan el juicio sin volverlo vago.

items.respuesta: The post makes an interesting point, but I think its conclusion needs more care. First, the writer seems to overlook the size of the sample: only thirty pupils from one class were asked, so the result may fall short of what a general claim requires. Second, the post rests on the idea that headphones stop fights, but it gives no evidence of how the fights were counted, which leaves the method open to question. To some extent, the fall in fights is likely to be linked to the headphones, although other factors, such as the weather or a new teacher, may also account for it. Arguably, the pupils who use headphones are simply the quiet ones, so the link is tenuous. Rather than handing out headphones in every school, a reasonable alternative would be to survey several classes for a whole term and compare the results. A balanced critique must also admit that the idea is worth testing, and I would certainly support a careful trial.

Second, the council says that the envelope was a gift for a school, and nobody has confirmed the blogger's version, which comes from an anonymous source. titulo.es: Verificar una historia viral paso a paso

texto.es: Verificar es un proceso, no una opinión. Paso 1: separa cada afirmación y evalúala por su cuenta (true, partly true, misleading, unproven, false). Paso 2: rastrea la historia hasta su fuente original y mira el contexto: un dato real puede estar out of context. Paso 3: señala qué evidencia falta (There is no evidence that…). Paso 4: redacta un veredicto matizado con rate as y una tentative conclusion. Si solo falta la prueba, no escribas false: escribe unproven.

When I read a student essay, I start with the last sentence of the introduction, because that is where the thesis usually sits. Then I read only the first sentence of each body paragraph. If those sentences, put together, tell a clear story, the outline is sound. If they jump from idea to idea, I already know where the essay needs work, before I have read a single example.
Many schools now face a difficult choice.
I will argue that homework should be shorter.
Second, short tasks help pupils to sleep.

Summer temperatures fell by two degrees in three towns.

Many towns now struggle with heat, dust and constant noise. I will argue that every town should plant more trees along its streets. First, trees make the air in the streets far cooler. Measurements in three towns show that summer temperatures fell by two degrees where trees were planted. Second, a shaded street is better for trade. Shops on tree-lined streets reported more customers, because people stopped to look at the windows. To sum up, the evidence suggests that streets with trees are cooler, quieter and busier. Towns that hesitate are choosing the problem over the solution.

The final paragraph of the essay reads like this. Libraries that close at six serve only those who finish work early, and the readers who need them most are left outside. titulo.es: Anatomía de un ensayo: tesis, frases temáticas y cierre

texto.es: Un ensayo de cinco párrafos tiene una estructura predecible. La introducción presenta el tema y termina con la thesis statement: la postura que todo el texto defiende. Cada body paragraph empieza con una topic sentence que anuncia su idea central, y el resto la supports con datos y ejemplos. La conclusión restates la tesis con otras palabras y cierra sin ideas nuevas. Si lees la tesis y la primera frase de cada párrafo, obtienes el outline completo del ensayo.
Tesis + frase temática + apoyo + cierre:

formula.texto: Cities should ban cars from their centres.

nota.es: tesis: la postura que se defiende

formula.texto: First, cars make the air dirtier.

nota.es: frase temática del primer párrafo

formula.texto: Figures from three cities show it.

nota.es: apoyo: datos que respaldan la idea

formula.texto: To sum up, centres are better without cars.

nota.es: conclusión: retoma la tesis

filas.texto: la postura que defiende el ensayo
retoma la tesis sin ideas nuevas

items.texto: A strong introduction hooks the reader and ends with a thesis statement, the sentence that tells us exactly what the essay will defend.

traduccion.es: Una buena introducción engancha al lector y termina con un enunciado de tesis, la frase que dice exactamente qué defenderá el ensayo.

nota.es: La tesis suele ocupar la última frase de la introducción.

items.texto: Each body paragraph opens with a topic sentence, so a reader who skims only first lines still sees what the essay argues.

traduccion.es: Cada párrafo de desarrollo abre con una frase temática, así que un lector que solo ojea las primeras líneas ve igualmente lo que el ensayo sostiene.

nota.es: Argues que + oración: el ensayo toma una postura.

items.texto: The rest of the paragraph supports that opening claim with evidence, examples and reasons, each one linked to the point above.

traduccion.es: El resto del párrafo respalda esa afirmación inicial con pruebas, ejemplos y razones, cada una enlazada con el punto anterior.

nota.es: Support (verbo) = dar pruebas o razones a favor de una idea.

items.texto: Good writers signpost their structure with phrases such as in the first place or by contrast, so readers never lose the thread.

traduccion.es: Los buenos autores señalizan su estructura con expresiones como «en primer lugar» o «por el contrario», y así los lectores nunca pierden el hilo.

nota.es: Signpost funciona como verbo: marca el camino al lector.

items.texto: A forceful conclusion restates the thesis in fresh words and can round off the essay without introducing a new argument.

traduccion.es: Una conclusión contundente reformula la tesis con palabras nuevas y puede cerrar el ensayo sin introducir un argumento nuevo.

nota.es: Restates = dice lo mismo con otras palabras; round off = cerrar de forma redonda.

items.texto: Before writing, draw up an outline to build a case for one position, because a plan shows at once which point is missing.

traduccion.es: Antes de escribir, elabora un esquema para argumentar a favor de una postura, porque un plan muestra enseguida qué punto falta.

nota.es: Build a case for + sustantivo: construir los argumentos de una postura.

items.texto: Many towns now struggle with heat, dust and constant noise. I will argue that every town should plant more trees along its streets. First, trees make the air in the streets far cooler. Shops on tree-lined streets reported more customers, because people stopped to look at the windows. To sum up, the evidence suggests that streets with trees are cooler, quieter and busier. Towns that hesitate are choosing the problem over the solution.

titulo.es: Señalar hacia atrás y hacia delante sin repetir

texto.es: Para no repetir palabras, el inglés escrito enlaza las frases con referencias. This/such a + sustantivo resume la idea anterior (such a decision); the former y the latter distinguen dos elementos citados, y respectively los empareja en el mismo orden. Con the same applies to y by the same token evitas repetir una frase entera; in doing so y thereby añaden una consecuencia. Hacia delante apuntan the following points. Regla de oro: si hay dos posibles antecedentes, repite el sustantivo para que la referencia sea clara.

Last year I wrote an email to my landlord that ran to three paragraphs. I explained, at length and with great feeling, that due to the fact that the heating had broken down, I had been forced to make the decision to move in with my brother. He never replied. When I showed the email to a friend, she asked me what I wanted. A repair, I said. Then write that, she answered. I trimmed the message to four lines, and the heating was fixed within two days. Admittedly, the short version felt less generous to me. Nevertheless, it worked far better.

Last year I decided to leave my hometown and study in another city. Admittedly, the choice was not easy, because my family lives there and I had never lived alone. Nevertheless, I wanted a course that my local college did not offer, so I got to the point and applied. At first I was homesick, and the flat was small and noisy. However, I soon found friends, and my classes were better than I expected. My parents were worried at first, but they supported me in the end. Looking back, I am glad that I trusted my own judgement, although I still miss my mother's cooking. Long version: Due to the fact that I wanted to save money, I made a decision to work at weekends. Concise version: Because I wanted to save money, I decided to work at weekends. Long version: In order to be able to concentrate, I turned off my phone at this point in time. Concise version: To concentrate, I turned off my phone.

items.audio: Last year I wrote an email to my landlord that ran to three paragraphs. I explained, at length and with great feeling, that due to the fact that the heating had broken down, I had been forced to make the decision to move in with my brother. He never replied. When I showed the email to a friend, she asked me what I wanted. A repair, I said. Then write that, she answered. I trimmed the message to four lines, and the heating was fixed within two days. Admittedly, the short version felt less generous to me. Nevertheless, it worked far better.

Every September the school publishes a new list of rules, and every September most of us read it once and forget it. I will argue that this happens not because we are lazy, but because we were never asked. Rules that pupils help to write are followed more willingly, because people defend what they have built. I will argue that the school should not ban phones at break, because a ban solves the wrong problem. First, pupils use their phones to talk to friends who are in other classes, and this contact is the only chance they have to do so. Second, a ban teaches pupils to hide their phones instead of using them well. Last term, for example, my class agreed on a simple rule and complaints fell by half. Admittedly, some pupils spend the whole break looking at a screen. Nevertheless, this is a problem of habits, not of phones, and, as mentioned above, a rule that pupils help to write is easier to respect. Some teachers take issue with this view, but a sensible alternative would be phone-free zones, which persuade without pushing anybody. I also believe that the school should trust us more, because trust is the best way to teach responsibility. In conclusion, the school should give us a say and trust us to use our phones well. In my opinion, the school should not take phones away at break, because a ban would hurt pupils who use them sensibly. First, many of us talk to friends from other classes, and this is often our only chance to do so. Second, a strict rule would teach us to hide our phones rather than to control them. Last year, for instance, our class made its own rule, and arguments about phones almost disappeared. It is true that some pupils stare at a screen for the whole break. Even so, this is a question of habits, and, as noted above, rules that pupils help to write are easier to respect. A reasonable alternative would be quiet zones, where phones are allowed only for messages. Some teachers take issue with this view, but I think it is fair to ask them for trust. In short, pupils deserve a say in this decision, and the magazine should keep asking for it. Revision: I trimmed two long sentences and removed a repeated example.

Method. The survey was conducted between March and May. titulo.es: Cómo se cuenta (y se lee) el método de un estudio

texto.es: Para describir un método, el inglés académico usa el pasivo en pasado: was conducted, were recruited, were asked to. Importa qué se hizo y a quién, no quién lo hizo. Un lector atento se pregunta además: ¿cómo se consiguió la muestra (recruited, randomly selected, at random)? ¿Cuántos respondieron (response rate)? ¿Qué garantías hubo (informed consent)? Y cuidado: «realizar» un estudio es conduct o carry out; realize significa «darse cuenta».
Muestra + was/were + participio + detalle del método:

A strong correlation does not demonstrate that one thing causes another, because a third factor may explain both.

The authors of a large survey found that people who use standing desks report less back pain. texto.es: Un buen lector separa tres capas: lo que los datos muestran (una correlación), lo que los autores sugieren (suggest, may) y lo que nadie ha demostrado (una relación causal). Our survey of two hundred pupils produced two main findings. First, sixty per cent of the pupils sleep less than eight hours a night. Second, among those who sleep little, twice as many girls as boys say that they feel tired in class. These figures suggest that a lack of sleep may affect how pupils feel at school, and they appear to show that girls are more affected than boys, at least to some extent. However, the results have an important limitation. All the pupils came from one school, and they described their own sleep, so the data may not be reliable. For this reason, we cannot say that sleep causes tiredness; we can only say that the two seem to be linked. Further research with a larger sample from several schools would be needed before anyone could generalise these results to all teenagers. We therefore treat them as a starting point, not as proof. In short, the findings stand out and deserve attention, but they should be read with caution.

titulo.es: Redactar hallazgos, límites y siguientes pasos

texto.es: Un párrafo de resultados sigue un orden: 1) hallazgos con cifras (two findings stand out: sixty per cent…); 2) interpretación con un verbo cauto (suggest, indicate, appear to, may); 3) un límite con however (una sola escuela, datos declarados, muestra pequeña); 4) el siguiente paso (further research would be needed). La cifra va sin the delante, y la conclusión debe ser más débil que los datos: to some extent, tend to, with caution.

We asked two hundred pupils about their sleep and found two things that stand out. To begin with, 60 per cent of them sleep for less than eight hours a night. In addition, among the pupils who sleep little, double the number of girls compared with boys reported feeling tired during lessons. The data indicate that a lack of sleep could affect how pupils feel at school, and girls seem to be more affected than boys to some extent. Nevertheless, there is a key limitation: only one school took part, and the pupils reported their own hours, so the answers may not be reliable. Because of this, the results do not show that sleep causes tiredness; they only point to a link. Further research with a larger sample from different schools would help us to see whether the same pattern appears elsewhere, and whether anyone can generalise from it. We therefore see them as a starting point, not as proof. To sum up, the findings are useful, but they must be treated with caution.

Last June a survey was conducted among three hundred residents of the old neighbourhood. The participants were selected at random from a list and were asked to complete a questionnaire online. Two results stand out. First, roughly a third of the residents said that the street lighting is poor, whereas the vast majority praised the park. Second, twice as many older residents as young ones feel unsafe at night. These findings suggest that lighting may be a top priority for the neighbourhood, and they appear to show that older people are more worried. However, there is an important limitation: most answers came from two streets, and the residents described their own feelings, so the data may be biased. For that reason, we cannot generalise the results to the whole city. As a next step, we propose a three-month trial run of new lamps in the two streets, and we suggest that the council should report the results in the autumn. Further research with a larger sample would then show whether the change really helped, and whether residents in other streets feel the same way.

traduccion.es: Cuando unos amigos entusiasmados se solapan, las frases se quedan a medias y el oyente tiene que reconstruir el significado con lo que queda.

nota.es: Overlap describe voces que suenan a la vez; trail off, una frase que se apaga sin terminar.

items.texto: Hang on, sorry to interrupt, but I thought the meeting had been moved to Friday, not to Thursday.

traduccion.es: Espera, perdona que interrumpa, pero pensaba que la reunión se había pasado al viernes, no al jueves.

nota.es: Hang on frena la conversación; sorry to interrupt pide permiso para cortar.

items.texto: We all talk over each other and interrupt constantly, so I sometimes lose the thread of what anyone is saying.

traduccion.es: Todos hablamos encima unos de otros y nos interrumpimos sin parar, así que a veces pierdo el hilo de lo que dice cada uno.

nota.es: Lose the thread = perder el hilo; talk over each other = hablar a la vez.

items.texto: Whenever Tom is on a roll, nobody can get a word in edgeways, so we chime in early and our voices overlap.

traduccion.es: Cuando Tom está lanzado, nadie logra meter una palabra, así que intervenimos pronto y nuestras voces se solapan.

nota.es: Get a word in edgeways = lograr decir algo cuando otro no para; chime in = intervenir de forma espontánea.

items.texto: Anyway, as I was saying, let us switch to the budget before the room gets too noisy to hear properly.

traduccion.es: En fin, como iba diciendo, pasemos al presupuesto antes de que la sala se ponga demasiado ruidosa para oír bien.

nota.es: As I was saying retoma lo dicho antes; switch to + tema cambia de tema a propósito.

items.texto: Sorry, did I cut in? Go ahead; I did not mean to interrupt, I simply got carried away.

traduccion.es: Perdona, ¿me metí en medio? Adelante; no quería interrumpir, simplemente me dejé llevar.

nota.es: Go ahead devuelve el turno a quien fue interrumpido; cut in = meterse a mitad de una frase ajena.

consigna.es: ¿Qué función cumple «hang on» en esta escena?

feedback.es: Hang on frena a Tom para comprobar un dato; no le cede el turno (eso sería go ahead) ni cambia de tema.

pista.es: Es una fórmula para frenar, no para seguir.

opciones: It invites Tom to carry on with the rest of his explanation.
It changes the subject to the invitation itself.
It stops the talk so that she can check something.
items.texto: Tom was halfway through giving the schedule when Mia said hang on, because the date he had just read out did not match the one on the invitation.

items.audio: Four flatmates were planning a surprise party, and nobody finished a sentence. Mia started to say that the cake should be ordered by Thursday, but Tom cut in to ask who was paying, and Carlos, talking over both of them, said he could pay if nobody minded waiting until the end of the month. Sara tried to get a word in edgeways, because the flat would be free only on Saturday, not on Friday, which changed everything. Mia laughed, said hang on, as she was saying, the cake came first, and asked Sara to go ahead. Sara repeated the date, and everyone agreed, although Carlos was still not sure about the money.

consigna.es: Escucha y elige qué sugiere la reacción final de Carlos.

feedback.es: «Still not sure about the money» indica que para él el tema del dinero seguía pendiente, aunque aceptó la fecha.

opciones: That the question of the money was still open.
That he could not attend the party on Saturday.
That he preferred to leave the planning to the others.

texto.es: El inglés se habla en decenas de países y cada variedad regional tiene su acento, su ritmo y algunas palabras propias, aunque comparte casi toda la gramática. Aquí practicas el léxico y las estructuras: prepone (India, «adelantar»), how far? y flash me (Nigeria), grand y «I am after + -ing» (Irlanda), arvo, reckon y heaps (Australia). Como la voz de la app es sintética, el acento lo irás afinando con hablantes reales. Si no entiendes una palabra, deduce por el contexto y quédate con la idea general.

items.texto: Because a regional variety is a full system, not a mistake, colloquial words such as arvo or heaps are perfectly normal there.

traduccion.es: Como una variedad regional es un sistema completo y no un error, palabras coloquiales como arvo o heaps son perfectamente normales allí.

nota.es: Colloquial = propio del habla cotidiana; arvo (tarde) y heaps (un montón) son rasgos del inglés australiano.

items.texto: In India a colleague may ask you to prepone tomorrow's meeting, which means moving it earlier, the opposite of postpone.

traduccion.es: En la India un colega puede pedirte que adelantes la reunión de mañana, lo que significa pasarla a una hora más temprana, lo contrario de postpone.

nota.es: Prepone es típico del inglés de la India: se forma por analogía con postpone.

items.texto: How far is a friendly greeting in Nigeria, and flash me means ring once and hang up so that I call you back.

traduccion.es: How far es un saludo amistoso en Nigeria, y flash me significa llamar una vez y colgar para que yo devuelva la llamada.

nota.es: How far? no pregunta por la distancia: equivale a «¿qué tal?»; flash funciona como verbo.

items.texto: An Irish speaker who says I am grand is fine, not big, and I am after finishing means that I have just finished.

traduccion.es: Un irlandés que dice I am grand está bien, no es grande, y I am after finishing significa que acabo de terminar.

nota.es: Grand = estupendo, bien; be after + -ing expresa una acción recién terminada.

traduccion.es: Un australiano podría decir Creo que tenemos un montón de tiempo esta tarde, y quien escucha pronto se da cuenta de estas palabras.

nota.es: Reckon = creer; pick up on = percibir algo que no se dice de forma explícita.

items.texto: Colloquial speech in every variety carries a distinctive lilt, and if you get the gist you can manage without every word.

traduccion.es: El habla coloquial de cada variedad tiene una cadencia característica, y si captas la idea general puedes arreglártelas sin entender cada palabra.

nota.es: Get the gist = entender lo esencial; lilt es el ritmo melódico de un acento.

titulo.es: Lo que se dice y lo que se quiere decir

texto.es: En inglés cotidiano, sobre todo con cortesía, lo importante suele quedar sin decir. Una pausa («Well…»), un suavizador (a bit, I suppose, hardly) o una respuesta vaga (I will think about it, we will see) suelen significar «no» o «no me convence». Pregúntate qué esperaba el oyente y si la respuesta lo cumple; si evita decir sí o no, probablemente es un no amable. Leer entre líneas es notar lo que falta: «It is a bit pricey» casi nunca habla solo del precio.
Pausa + suavizador + respuesta vaga = rechazo amable:

items.texto: “Well, it is a bit pricey, so I will think about it” is a polite way of saying that the shopper will probably not buy.

traduccion.es: «Bueno, es un poco caro, así que lo pensaré» es una forma cortés de decir que quien compra probablemente no comprará.

nota.es: Dice «es caro» pero quiere decir «probablemente no»; la pausa y a bit suavizan el rechazo.

items.texto: “I suppose it could work” is what people say when they accept an idea without any enthusiasm at all.

traduccion.es: «Supongo que podría funcionar» es lo que se dice cuando se acepta una idea sin ningún entusiasmo.

nota.es: I suppose suena a aceptar sin ganas: el hablante no está convencido.

items.texto: Honest friends still try to let someone down gently, so a refusal often hides inside a compliment.

traduccion.es: Los amigos sinceros también intentan rechazar con tacto, así que un rechazo suele esconderse dentro de un cumplido.

nota.es: Let someone down gently = rechazar sin herir; el «no» se disfraza de elogio.

items.texto: “It is not exactly what the client wanted, but we will see” suggests real doubt, not a promise.

traduccion.es: «No es exactamente lo que quería el cliente, pero ya veremos» sugiere una duda real, no una promesa.

nota.es: Not exactly equivale casi a «no»; we will see muestra dudas, no un compromiso.

items.texto: You learn to read between the lines when someone hardly answers the question and quickly changes the subject.

traduccion.es: Aprendes a leer entre líneas cuando alguien apenas responde a la pregunta y cambia rápido de tema.

nota.es: Hardly (apenas) y un cambio de tema son señales de una respuesta evasiva.

items.texto: Honest speakers who beat around the bush are rarely lying; to put it mildly, they just dislike saying no.

traduccion.es: Quienes se andan por las ramas rara vez mienten; por decirlo suavemente, simplemente les disgusta decir que no.

nota.es: Beat around the bush = no ir al grano; to put it mildly suaviza una crítica fuerte.

consigna.es: ¿Qué quiere decir realmente esta respuesta?

feedback.es: La pausa y un adjetivo vago («certainly different») suavizan una opinión poco entusiasta.

pista.es: Las pausas y los adjetivos vagos suelen suavizar una crítica.

opciones: She is delighted and wants to copy it.

consigna.es: Completa: «Supongo que podría funcionar, aunque yo habría elegido otro.»

feedback.es: I suppose it could work expresa una aceptación sin entusiasmo: la frase siguiente lo confirma.

consigna.es: Relaciona cada respuesta con lo que probablemente quiere decir el hablante.

feedback.es: Cada respuesta indirecta esconde un mensaje: rechazo por el precio, un no amable, aceptación fría o falta de compromiso.

pista.es: Pregúntate qué respuesta evita decir sí o no.

feedback.es: Con «I suppose», «hardly» y «let us see» suaviza una opinión clara: el borrador no está listo; no lo considera casi terminado ni pide solo una segunda opinión.

items.audio: At the garden centre, Mia held up a lamp and asked Tom whether it was any good. Tom looked at the price tag and said that it was a bit pricey, but certainly bright. When Tom asked whether she was going to buy it, Mia said that she would think about it, put the lamp back on the shelf and headed for the door. Outside, Tom admitted that he could hardly say he loved the colour either, and they both laughed. The assistant, who had heard everything, pretended to tidy a shelf.

feedback.es: Hardly suaviza una crítica: Tom no está entusiasmado con el color, y ese «either» conecta su opinión con la reticencia de Mia, lo que explica que ambos se rían.

opciones: That he liked the colour but hid it to be polite.

The lecturer began by saying that she wanted to look at why some companies are trying a four-day working week, and she then outlined three main reasons. According to her, the first reason is that staff are more focused when a long weekend is coming, and the work done stayed the same at one firm in Bristol. The second reason is that sick days fell sharply, by about a third in a year. The third reason is that it became easier to recruit, because candidates see the shorter week as a sign of trust. By way of illustration, she described a company that reduced its hours from forty to thirty-two without cutting pay. She went on to draw attention to a limit: the change is not suitable for every kind of business, since hospitals and shops cannot simply close on Fridays. In short, the lecturer said that the four-day week works best where results, not hours, can be measured, and she did not suggest that every company should copy it.

Good morning. Today I want to look at why some companies are trying a four-day working week. There are three main reasons. First, managers report that staff are more focused when they know a long weekend is coming, and one firm in Bristol found that the work done stayed the same after the change. Second, sick days fell sharply, by about a third in a year. Third, it became easier to recruit, because candidates see the shorter week as a sign of trust. By way of illustration, one company reduced its hours from forty to thirty-two without cutting pay. However, the change is not suitable for every kind of business; hospitals and shops cannot simply close on Fridays. In short, the four-day week works best where results can be measured, not hours.

explicacion.es: Resume significa «reanudar». Para resumir se usa to summarise o in short.

texto.es: Al escuchar una charla, apunta solo lo esencial: el tema, dos o tres ideas principales, algún dato concreto (cifras, nombres) y la conclusión. Las señales del orador (first, however, in short) te guían. Para resumir, atribuye lo que se dijo (The lecturer outlined…, According to her…, She went on to…), reformula con tus palabras y cierra con In short o To summarise. Un resumen fiel no incluye datos inventados ni tu opinión. Ojo: resume en inglés significa «reanudar», no «resumir».

In this episode, the host asked her guest about working from home, and the guest came across as thoughtful rather than certain.

texto.es: Un episodio de pódcast se trabaja en cuatro pasos: 1) toma notas mientras escuchas; 2) resume con fidelidad lo que se dijo (The host asked…, According to the guest…); 3) señala la implicación, lo que parece dar a entender sin decirlo (seem to imply: una respuesta corta o vaga puede decir más de lo que parece); 4) añade tu reacción con matiz (to be fair, I take issue with…, I would add…, up to a point). Most learners read their corrections and promise to be more careful, which is precisely the wrong lesson. Care is not the issue. A sentence such as the increase of prices worried us is not careless; it simply reflects a rule that was never absorbed. En este nivel los deslices caen en cinco categorías: gramática oral (That film, it was brilliant), concesión (Much as I admire her, I disagree), tacto (I was wondering whether…), registro académico (the increase in prices) y estilo narrativo (had already started). items.audio: Mia's tutor has just finished marking her last four drafts. Fourteen marks in total, he says, but only six of them are careless slips: a dropped article here, a missing plural there, the kind of thing Mia corrects herself as soon as she reads them again. The other eight are different. Three times she wrote the increase of prices, twice she added but after much as, and three times she opened a request with a direct question. According to the tutor, nobody should lose sleep over the slips, whereas the recurring errors deserve a proper diagnosis, because they show rules she has never really absorbed.

When we drafted our style guide last spring, several of us argued for a single pattern, and I was one of them. The guide now says that every contingency clause must begin with should, and I still see the logic: the pattern is short and formal. In an email to a colleague, though, Should it rain, the match will be postponed can sound stiff. I would keep the rule for contracts and reports, and leave emails free to use a plain if. Asking every reader to accept one pattern would only make our writing less natural. Having tested it on real emails, I have changed my mind.

texto.es: Reparar es cambiar solo lo necesario. Marca el error, nombra la regla y toca únicamente las palabras que fallan: un pronombre olvidado (That film, it was brilliant), un conector que sobra (Much as I admire her, I disagree), un orden mal puesto (However expensive the ticket is…), una condición formal (Should demand fall, …), una preposición equivocada (the demand for tickets) o un tiempo que rompe la secuencia (had already left). Después relee la frase entera: si suena natural y conserva tu voz, está reparada. Reescribir de más puede introducir errores nuevos.

vocabulario.texto: In song lyrics, figurative language works through metaphor: a paper boat on a grey river is never literal.
To read between the lines, ask what the singer avoids saying, because the lyrics often imply more than any single verse states.
A hint of regret can sit inside a cheerful verse: the singer says I am fine, yet the tone quietly contradicts her.
A faint echo in an empty room can evoke absence, since a sound that returns without an answer suggests that someone has left.
Understated lyrics may strike a chord because they never name the feeling: the listener supplies it, and the metaphor does the rest.
Separate what is literal from what is implied: a phone left face up beside the plate may suggest that someone is expecting a call.

A radio presenter introduces the second verse of Last Bus Home. The singer says that she is not angry, only learning how long the last bus takes to come. The presenter points out that the word only makes the complaint smaller on purpose, so that the listener senses patience rather than anger.

The final verse of Last Bus Home is only four lines long. The singer folds a timetable into her pocket, turns off the hall light and says, to the empty hall, that some doors are better left unlocked. Nothing in the verse mentions the person who left. Critics have noticed that the word tomorrow appears in every verse except this one, and that its absence makes the ending feel quieter, less hopeful and more final. Yet the unlocked door suggests that the singer has not entirely given up. It is, the host concludes, a song that refuses to explain itself, and that is exactly why people keep arguing about it.

Some listeners hear Last Bus Home as a sad song about a break-up. I hear something less obvious: the singer never blames anyone, and the simple language she uses keeps the feeling in check. Sadness, here, is handled like weather: noticed, described, accepted. It is a song about patience more than loss.

titulo.es: Lo que dice la letra y lo que sugiere

texto.es: Una letra casi nunca lo dice todo. El significado literal es lo que dicen las palabras (a door); el figurado, lo que quieren decir (una promesa que no se cumple). Además, una letra puede implicar cosas que nunca nombra: un teléfono boca arriba sugiere que alguien espera una llamada. Para interpretarla: busca la metáfora, traduce la imagen a una idea, fíjate en el tono (suave, irónico, resignado) y decide qué se insinúa sin decirse. Apoya siempre tu lectura en una palabra concreta del texto y distingue el tono del narrador del tuyo.

items.texto: In song lyrics, figurative language works through metaphor: a paper boat on a grey river is never literal.

traduccion.es: En las letras de canciones, el lenguaje figurado funciona mediante la metáfora: un barquito de papel en un río gris nunca es literal.

nota.es: Lo literal es lo que dicen las palabras; lo figurado, lo que quieren decir. Una imagen imposible o rara suele pedir lectura figurada.

items.texto: To read between the lines, ask what the singer avoids saying, because the lyrics often imply more than any single verse states.

nota.es: Imply: la letra sugiere algo que nunca dice con todas las letras; lo que se calla también comunica.

items.texto: A hint of regret can sit inside a cheerful verse: the singer says I am fine, yet the tone quietly contradicts her.

traduccion.es: Un matiz de pesar puede esconderse en una estrofa alegre: la cantante dice «estoy bien», pero el tono la contradice sin alzar la voz.

nota.es: El tono (suave, irónico, resignado) se deduce de las palabras elegidas y de lo que no encaja con ellas.

items.texto: A faint echo in an empty room can evoke absence, since a sound that returns without an answer suggests that someone has left.

traduccion.es: Un eco tenue en una habitación vacía puede evocar ausencia, porque un sonido que vuelve sin respuesta sugiere que alguien se ha ido.

nota.es: Un sonido o un espacio vacío insinúan una ausencia sin nombrarla.

items.texto: Understated lyrics may strike a chord because they never name the feeling: the listener supplies it, and the metaphor does the rest.

traduccion.es: Una letra contenida puede tocar la fibra porque nunca nombra el sentimiento: lo pone el oyente y la metáfora hace el resto.

nota.es: Understated = dicho con contención; el efecto emocional nace de lo que el oyente completa.

items.texto: Separate what is literal from what is implied: a phone left face up beside the plate may suggest that someone is expecting a call.

items.audio: The final verse of Last Bus Home is only four lines long. The singer folds a timetable into her pocket, turns off the hall light and says, to the empty hall, that some doors are better left unlocked. Nothing in the verse mentions the person who left. Critics have noticed that the word tomorrow appears in every verse except this one, and that its absence makes the ending feel quieter, less hopeful and more final. Yet the unlocked door suggests that the singer has not entirely given up. It is, the host concludes, a song that refuses to explain itself, and that is exactly why people keep arguing about it.

Rain tapped the window of the night bus. Tom counted his coins twice, and then a third time, while his foot beat the floor. Behind him, a man in a grey suit sighed at his own watch. On Tom's knees lay the folder with his drawings, and his hands would not stay still. The driver hummed a cheerful song, which made everything worse. Off the bus he jumped, and up the stairs he ran. Silence in the corridor. A closed door. He was sure he had missed the interview by ten minutes, and he had practised his speech all week. Then a woman appeared at the end of the hall, holding a cup of tea. "Are you Tom?" she asked. "We had to postpone everything. The director, of course, is stuck in traffic." Tom laughed so loudly that the secretary looked up. It turned out that the director had been sitting behind him on the bus all along, and he arrived five minutes later, out of breath, blaming the driver's song. In the end, Tom got the job, and the driver got a thank-you card.

items.respuesta: Rain tapped the window of the night bus. Tom counted his coins twice, and then a third time, while his foot beat the floor. Behind him, a man in a grey suit sighed at his own watch. On Tom's knees lay the folder with his drawings, and his hands would not stay still. The driver hummed a cheerful song, which made everything worse. Off the bus he jumped, and up the stairs he ran. Silence in the corridor. A closed door. He was sure he had missed the interview by ten minutes, and he had practised his speech all week. Then a woman appeared at the end of the hall, holding a cup of tea. "Are you Tom?" she asked. "We had to postpone everything. The director, of course, is stuck in traffic." Tom laughed so loudly that the secretary looked up. It turned out that the director had been sitting behind him on the bus all along, and he arrived five minutes later, out of breath, blaming the driver's song. In the end, Tom got the job, and the driver got a thank-you card.

Every Sunday my grandfather fished at the lake, and every Sunday he came home with an empty bucket and a happy face. My mother laughed and said that fishing was only an excuse to sit in silence. One morning I followed him. Into the water went his line, and out of the silence came nothing. Hours passed. Nobody spoke, and even the gulls seemed to be waiting for something to happen. The lake stayed as still as a painting. Then a tiny silver fish jumped into the bucket by itself. My grandfather stared at it. His hands shook a little as he lifted the bucket. I had never seen him so excited, or so suspicious. "Of course," he said at last, "the day I bring a friend, the fish behave." It turned out that he had been hiding a secret all along: he had never caught a single fish, and he was delighted about it. In the end, he let the fish go and told everybody it was the best catch of his life. Since then, he has never fished alone.

I would like to put forward a proposal for the open day: a story workshop in the square. By last spring, the square had been empty for months, and many neighbours told me they missed a place to meet. A workshop with a small book stall could change that. The square belongs to all of us, and a story is the cheapest way to fill it. I know that a new idea always raises questions, and I welcome them, because a fair point can only improve the plan. I understand that the budget is tight, and much as I appreciate your concern, I believe we can manage. I was wondering whether the volunteers could bring the books and the chairs, so the cost would be almost nothing, and nobody would need to spend money on anything else. Should it rain, we will move the workshop into the hall. Failing that, we can shorten the morning. If everyone agrees, I will confirm the stall by Friday, and by Saturday we will have prepared the posters. Shall we agree on that? Thank you for listening, and I hope you will join us.

titulo.es: La jornada abierta: todo en una intervención

texto.es: La simulación pide combinar lo del bloque en una sola intervención: presentas una idea con un breve contexto narrativo (By last spring, the square had been empty…), la defiendes ante una objeción con concesión y tacto (Much as I appreciate…, I was wondering whether…), anticipas imprevistos (Should it rain, …) y cierras con un plan y un plazo (By Friday, we will have…). Antes de entregar, revisa como en la clase 92: marca el error, repara lo mínimo y comprueba el registro. Recuerda que una buena intervención se lee también entre líneas: lo que callas pesa.

Let me put forward a proposal: a story workshop for the open day. When I was a child, the square used to be full of people, and I would love to see that again. Stories can bring neighbours together, and a simple workshop is a good way to start. I also believe that a workshop like this costs very little and gives a lot back. Nobody needs a big stage to tell a story, only a few chairs and a little time. Fair enough, the budget is limited. Much as I would like a bigger stall, I am sure the volunteers can help, and I was wondering whether the library could lend us some books for the morning. In the event of rain, the workshop will take place in the hall. By Friday I will have confirmed the stall with the council, and the posters will be ready by Saturday. That is our deadline, and I am confident that we can meet it together. Are we all happy with this plan? Thank you for listening, and I hope that many of you will come and tell a story of your own.

I would like to propose a workshop where neighbours write a short story together, one sentence each. The idea came from last year, when a stranger left a notebook on a bench and within a week the whole street had filled it. I understand that some of you worry about the noise and the cost, and I accept that both are fair points. Much as I am keen on the idea, I would not want it to divide us. I was wondering whether we could try it for one morning, with a small stall and a handful of volunteers, and then decide. Should the weather turn bad, we can use the library. By Friday I will have spoken to the volunteers, and by the following Friday we will have a clear answer. If the morning goes badly, at least we will have tried. I am not asking for a big budget, only for one morning and a little goodwill from all of us. Does that seem a fair compromise? Thank you for listening, and please tell me what you think before we vote.

The thesis of an opinion article is the central claim its writer defends, and it usually sits in the opening paragraph or returns, sharpened, in the last sentence.
A writer's stance shows in small choices: a phrase such as I would argue or I am not convinced reveals how firmly an opinion is held and how much room is left for doubt.
Writers concede a point before they answer it: Much as I understand the worry, the evidence points the other way, and my conclusion stands.
A rhetorical question does not seek information; it invites readers to reach the writer's own answer, as in: What, then, should adults do, if not simply wait?
Careful authors add a caveat to every sweeping claim, since a single counterexample could undermine a statement such as all screens damage children.
The implication of a closing sentence is often the most persuasive part of an essay: children whose minds wander and who never meet boredom may struggle to sit with themselves.
Children who are never bored miss a chance to invent.
Long afternoons with nothing to do please almost everyone, whatever their age.
Children should be spared every idle afternoon they dread.

Nobody enjoys a long afternoon with nothing to do, and I do not pretend otherwise. Yet I would argue that children who are never bored miss something important, because boredom is where new ideas begin.

It would be wrong to think that every child will turn a quiet hour into a masterpiece. Nevertheless, children who have never learned to sit with themselves may find it hard to sit with anything else, whether a difficult book, a long conversation or their own thoughts.

Some parents will object that boredom is a waste of time, and I understand the worry. Nobody enjoys a long afternoon with nothing to do. Yet I would argue that children who are never bored miss something important. Several studies suggest that bored children tend to invent games, draw and ask better questions, although it would be wrong to claim that every bored child will. The caveat matters: I am not saying that screens are damaging in themselves. What, then, should adults do? Nothing, mostly. Leave the silence alone, and something more interesting may grow there.
