titulo.es: Leer un artículo de opinión como analista

texto.es: Para analizar un texto largo de opinión no basta con entenderlo: hay que interrogarlo. ¿Cuál es la tesis? ¿Qué postura revelan los verbos y las cautelas (I would argue, tend to)? ¿Dónde concede el autor un punto antes de rebatirlo? ¿Qué recurso usa, como una pregunta retórica? ¿Qué salvedad limita sus afirmaciones y cuál deja sin límite? Y, sobre todo, ¿qué implica sin decirlo? Localiza cada respuesta en una frase concreta: sin evidencia textual, tu análisis es solo una opinión.
Analizar un artículo de opinión:

nota.es: la afirmación central del autor
concesión y refutación

formula.texto: The rhetorical question steers the reader towards…

nota.es: el recurso y su efecto
lo que se sugiere sin decirlo

filas.texto: Much as I understand the worry, …
Of course, that does not mean every bored child will.
…may find it hard to sit with anything else.

items.texto: The thesis of an opinion article is the central claim its writer defends, and it usually sits in the opening paragraph or returns, sharpened, in the last sentence.

traduccion.es: La tesis de un artículo de opinión es la afirmación central que defiende su autor, y suele estar en el párrafo inicial o volver, más afilada, en la última frase.

nota.es: No confundas la tesis con lo que el autor solo admite: lo admitido suele ir antes de yet o but.

items.texto: A writer's stance shows in small choices: a phrase such as I would argue or I am not convinced reveals how firmly an opinion is held and how much room is left for doubt.

traduccion.es: La postura de quien escribe se nota en pequeñas decisiones: una fórmula como «yo diría que» o «no me convence» revela con qué firmeza se sostiene una opinión y cuánto margen queda para la duda.

nota.es: Las fórmulas de postura y los modales (would, may) miden la seguridad del autor.

items.texto: Writers concede a point before they answer it: Much as I understand the worry, the evidence points the other way, and my conclusion stands.

traduccion.es: Quien escribe concede un punto antes de responderlo: Aunque entiendo la preocupación, la evidencia apunta en sentido contrario, y mi conclusión se mantiene.

nota.es: Conceder no cambia la postura: prepara el terreno para la refutación.

items.texto: A rhetorical question does not seek information; it invites readers to reach the writer's own answer, as in: What, then, should adults do, if not simply wait?

traduccion.es: Una pregunta retórica no busca información; invita al lector a llegar a la respuesta del propio autor, como en: ¿Qué deberían hacer, entonces, los adultos, sino esperar?

nota.es: Fíjate en quién responde: si el autor contesta su propia pregunta, su función es guiar al lector.

items.texto: Careful authors add a caveat to every sweeping claim, since a single counterexample could undermine a statement such as all screens damage children.

traduccion.es: Los autores cuidadosos añaden una salvedad a cada afirmación demasiado general, porque un solo contraejemplo podría socavar una frase como «todas las pantallas dañan a los niños».

nota.es: Una salvedad (of course, that does not mean…) protege la tesis; sin ella, la afirmación es fácil de derribar.

items.texto: The implication of a closing sentence is often the most persuasive part of an essay: children whose minds wander and who never meet boredom may struggle to sit with themselves.

traduccion.es: La implicación de una frase final suele ser la parte más persuasiva de un ensayo: los niños cuya mente divaga y que nunca conocen el aburrimiento pueden tener dificultad para estar a solas consigo mismos.

nota.es: La implicación es lo que sugiere el texto sin decirlo; pregúntate qué quiere que concluya el lector.

consigna.es: Localiza la tesis: ¿qué defiende realmente la autora de este párrafo?

feedback.es: La tesis llega tras «Yet I would argue»; lo anterior es lo que la autora admite sin cambiar de postura.

pista.es: La tesis es la afirmación que defiende, no la que concede al principio.

opciones: Children who are never bored miss a chance to invent.
Long afternoons with nothing to do please almost everyone, whatever their age.
Children should be spared every idle afternoon they dread.
items.texto: Nobody enjoys a long afternoon with nothing to do, and I do not pretend otherwise. Yet I would argue that children who are never bored miss something important, because boredom is where new ideas begin.

consigna.es: Completa: «Decir que todo daña es una afirmación demasiado general.»

feedback.es: Un sweeping claim abarca más de lo que puede demostrar; por eso un solo contraejemplo lo derriba.

pista.es: Adjetivo que describe una afirmación que lo abarca todo.

items.texto: To say that every screen harms every child is a ___ claim; one counterexample would be enough to rebut it.

consigna.es: Ordena: «Los niños aburridos suelen inventar juegos y hacer mejores preguntas.»

feedback.es: Tend to + verbo base expresa una tendencia: el autor matiza en lugar de afirmar que siempre ocurre.

pista.es: El sujeto va primero; tend to lleva el verbo en forma base.

items.respuesta: Bored children tend to invent games and ask better questions

consigna.es: ¿Qué actitud muestra la autora ante la prohibición de los celulares en clase?

feedback.es: Concede algo con «may help a little» y no la descarta, pero «treats the symptom» revela que duda de que resuelva el problema de fondo.

opciones: She welcomes it as the decisive answer to falling results.
She grants it some use but doubts that it tackles the real problem.
She rejects it as damaging and refuses to consider it.
She has no view of her own and only reports what others say.
items.texto: I am not convinced that banning phones in classrooms will raise results. It may help a little, and I would not rule it out, but a ban treats the symptom and leaves the cause alone.

consigna.es: Escucha y elige qué efecto busca la pregunta retórica de la autora.

feedback.es: La autora contesta su propia pregunta; no pide información, sino que guía al lector hacia su tesis.

opciones: To collect suggestions from readers who might disagree with her views.
To admit that she has no practical advice to offer readers.
To lead the reader to a conclusion she has already reached.
items.audio: What, then, should adults do? Hand over a tablet, and the problem disappears for ten minutes. Leave the silence alone, and something more interesting may grow. She does not wait for an answer. She supplies it, and the reader, having followed her this far, is ready to nod.

consigna.es: Relaciona cada frase del artículo con la función que cumple en el argumento.

feedback.es: Cada frase desempeña un papel distinto: postura explícita, concesión, pregunta retórica, exceso y reserva.

pares: I would argue that boredom is more useful than it seems
Admittedly, some screens have their uses
Is that really too much to ask?
Every screen ruins a child's concentration
Several studies suggest, though none proves, a link

contexto.es: Ana y Leo leen en clase un artículo de opinión sobre el aburrimiento y comparan sus subrayados.

dialogo.texto: I have marked the thesis: children should be bored sometimes. The writer also adds a caveat, so the claim is not sweeping.

traduccion.es: He marcado la tesis: los niños deberían aburrirse a veces. El autor añade además una salvedad, así que la afirmación no es demasiado general.

dialogo.texto: Right. And look at the opening: Much as I understand the worry. That is a concession, but the stance does not change.

traduccion.es: Exacto. Y mira el comienzo: Aunque entiendo la preocupación. Eso es una concesión, pero la postura no cambia.

dialogo.texto: So the last question is rhetorical? What, then, should adults do?

traduccion.es: Entonces, ¿la última pregunta es retórica? ¿Qué deberían hacer, entonces, los adultos?

dialogo.texto: Yes. It is persuasive because it leads us to the answer the writer already has in mind.

traduccion.es: Sí. Es persuasiva porque nos lleva a la respuesta que el autor ya tiene en mente.

consigna.es: Según el diálogo, ¿por qué resulta persuasiva la pregunta final del autor?

feedback.es: Leo explica que la pregunta nos lleva a «the answer the writer already has in mind»: por eso es retórica y persuasiva.

opciones.es: Porque conduce al lector hacia la respuesta que el autor ya tiene.
Porque el autor admite que no conoce la respuesta.
Porque repite la concesión con la que empieza el artículo.

consigna.es: ¿Qué da a entender la autora en la última frase, sin decirlo abiertamente?

feedback.es: El texto sugiere, sin afirmarlo, que quien nunca se queda a solas tendrá dificultades para concentrarse después; la primera frase descarta lo contrario.

opciones: That a quiet hour always produces creative work in every child.
That difficult books and long talks are unsuitable for children.
That children who read little are bound to think poorly.
That constant activity may leave children struggling to concentrate later.
items.texto: It would be wrong to think that every child will turn a quiet hour into a masterpiece. Nevertheless, children who have never learned to sit with themselves may find it hard to sit with anything else, whether a difficult book, a long conversation or their own thoughts.

consigna.es: Escucha el fragmento y elige la actitud de la autora ante los padres preocupados.

feedback.es: Comprende la preocupación de los padres, pero el «Yet I would argue» mantiene su tesis: empatía sin cesión.

opciones: Understanding enough to soften her main thesis quite a lot.
Understanding, but not ready to move from her main point.
Impatient with them for ignoring the evidence available to everyone.
items.audio: Some parents will object that boredom is a waste of time, and I understand the worry. Nobody enjoys a long afternoon with nothing to do. Yet I would argue that children who are never bored miss something important. Several studies suggest that bored children tend to invent games, draw and ask better questions, although it would be wrong to claim that every bored child will. The caveat matters: I am not saying that screens are damaging in themselves. What, then, should adults do? Nothing, mostly. Leave the silence alone, and something more interesting may grow there.

consigna.es: Completa: «Un solo contraejemplo bastaría para debilitar todo el argumento.»

feedback.es: Undermine es el verbo habitual para un argumento al que se le quita su base; un sweeping claim es muy vulnerable a él.

items.texto: Suppose the writer claimed that boredom always produces creativity. One counterexample would be enough to ___ the whole argument.

consigna.es: Resume en inglés la postura de la autora: su tesis y la objeción que concede.

feedback.es: Un buen resumen atribuye la tesis con un verbo de postura y deja visible la concesión sin perder la refutación.

items.respuesta: The writer argues that children should be bored sometimes. Much as she admits that boredom is hard for children, she maintains that it helps them to invent and to reflect.
aceptadas: The writer argues that children should be bored sometimes. Much as she admits that boredom is hard for children, she maintains that it helps them to invent and to reflect.
The author claims that bored children become more inventive. Although she admits that boredom is dull, she still believes that it helps children to reflect.
The writer maintains that children need some boredom. Much as she accepts that it can be dull, she argues that it helps children to invent more.
items.texto: Artículo «Let Them Be Bored». Defiende que los niños deben aburrirse a veces para inventar y reflexionar. Reconoce que el aburrimiento resulta incómodo. Escribe dos frases con un verbo de postura y una concesión (Much as…).

objetivo.es: Editar un borrador con precisión: corregir tiempos, registro, cohesión, conectores y concisión eligiendo el cambio mínimo.

We edit in layers: meaning first, then cohesion, then wording, and a final proofread for the slips that survive every earlier pass.
A connector must mirror the real logic of the ideas: in We cut the price; as a result, sales rose, it signals consequence, whereas however would suggest an unexpected contrast.
A wordy sentence buries its point, so tighten up the draft: In order to finish, we need time becomes To finish, we need time, and the meaning is untouched.
Needless repetition makes a sentence wordy: the recently opened shop carries the whole idea, whereas the new, recently opened shop says it twice.
A lapse in tense is easy to miss, so keep the timeline steady: when the manager arrived, the team had already finished the report and sent it to the council.
Colloquial phrasing and vague quantities weaken a report, and ambiguity is best removed with exact wording: forty interviews, not a lot of interviews.

explicacion.es: El conector fijo es on the other hand; la preposición in es un calco de «por otra parte».

titulo.es: Editar con precisión, capa por capa

texto.es: Editar con precisión es revisar por capas y elegir siempre el cambio mínimo. Ante cada marca, nombra la capa: (1) tiempo: ¿qué ocurrió antes?; (2) registro: ¿es demasiado coloquial para quien lo lee?; (3) cohesión: ¿a qué se refiere this o such?; (4) conector: ¿suma, contrasta o da resultado?; (5) concisión: ¿sobran palabras o repeticiones? Corrige solo lo necesario y relee la frase entera para comprobar que sigue sonando a ti y que no ha aparecido un nuevo desliz.
Corregir una marca de error:

nota.es: encuentras la palabra o la relación que falla
tiempo, registro, cohesión, conector o concisión
cambias lo mínimo que arregla el problema
compruebas que suena natural y que no hay un nuevo desliz

items.texto: We edit in layers: meaning first, then cohesion, then wording, and a final proofread for the slips that survive every earlier pass.

traduccion.es: Editamos por capas: primero el significado, después la cohesión, luego la redacción y, al final, una relectura para detectar los deslices que sobreviven a todas las pasadas anteriores.

nota.es: Revisar todo a la vez hace perder errores; cada capa tiene su propia pregunta.

items.texto: A connector must mirror the real logic of the ideas: in We cut the price; as a result, sales rose, it signals consequence, whereas however would suggest an unexpected contrast.

traduccion.es: Un conector debe reflejar la lógica real de las ideas: en Bajamos el precio; como resultado, las ventas subieron, señala consecuencia, mientras que however sugeriría un contraste inesperado.

nota.es: Suma (moreover), contrasta (however) o da resultado (as a result): elige según la relación real.

items.texto: A wordy sentence buries its point, so tighten up the draft: In order to finish, we need time becomes To finish, we need time, and the meaning is untouched.

traduccion.es: Una frase prolija entierra su idea, así que ajusta el borrador: In order to finish, we need time pasa a To finish, we need time, y el significado queda intacto.

nota.es: Si puedes quitar palabras sin perder significado, la frase estaba inflada.

items.texto: Needless repetition makes a sentence wordy: the recently opened shop carries the whole idea, whereas the new, recently opened shop says it twice.

traduccion.es: La repetición innecesaria vuelve prolija una frase: the recently opened shop contiene toda la idea, mientras que the new, recently opened shop la dice dos veces.

nota.es: New y recently opened cuentan la misma idea: basta con uno de los dos.

items.texto: A lapse in tense is easy to miss, so keep the timeline steady: when the manager arrived, the team had already finished the report and sent it to the council.

traduccion.es: Un desliz en el tiempo verbal es fácil de pasar por alto, así que mantén estable la cronología: cuando llegó el jefe, el equipo ya había terminado el informe y se lo había enviado al consejo.

nota.es: Lo anterior a otro hecho pasado lleva had + participio; no mezcles tiempos sin motivo.

items.texto: Colloquial phrasing and vague quantities weaken a report, and ambiguity is best removed with exact wording: forty interviews, not a lot of interviews.

traduccion.es: La redacción coloquial y las cantidades vagas debilitan un informe, y la ambigüedad se elimina mejor con palabras exactas: cuarenta entrevistas, no muchas entrevistas.

nota.es: El registro profesional prefiere cifras y expresiones precisas a fórmulas de conversación.

objetivo.es: Valorar una actuación oral modelo con una rúbrica de cuatro criterios: estructura, precisión, tacto y evidencia.

vocabulario.texto: rubric
criterion
structure
accuracy
tact
strength
weakness
assess
coherent
shortcoming
digress
cite
A rubric sets out the criteria by which we assess a performance, so that a verdict rests on evidence rather than on mood.
The first criterion is structure: a coherent talk opens with a clear purpose, develops two or three reasons in order, and closes by drawing them together.
The second criterion is accuracy, and any shortcoming here, such as a slip in tense or a misused connector, is judged by how far it blurs the message.
Tact is the third: a skilled speaker concedes a point and softens a request, and does not digress into blame or complaint.
The fourth criterion is evidence: a speaker who can cite a survey, a figure or a precise example is harder to ignore than one who says that many people agree.
A fair verdict names a strength and a weakness, and it quotes the exact words that prove each one.
Tact: it softens a difficult request for the audience.

texto.es: Valorar una actuación modelo es aplicar criterios, no dar una impresión. Usa una rúbrica de cuatro: estructura (apertura, razones, cierre), precisión (tiempos, conectores, orden), tacto (concesión, peticiones suaves, plan alternativo) y evidencia (datos y ejemplos). Para cada criterio cita la frase exacta que lo demuestra y decide si es una fortaleza o una debilidad. Un buen veredicto pesa ambas y no se deja llevar por el tono de voz ni por la simpatía del orador.

items.texto: A rubric sets out the criteria by which we assess a performance, so that a verdict rests on evidence rather than on mood.

traduccion.es: Una rúbrica establece los criterios con los que valoramos una actuación, de modo que el veredicto se apoye en pruebas y no en el estado de ánimo.

nota.es: Valorar con criterios evita las impresiones vagas del tipo «me gustó» o «me aburrió».

items.texto: The first criterion is structure: a coherent talk opens with a clear purpose, develops two or three reasons in order, and closes by drawing them together.

traduccion.es: El primer criterio es la estructura: una charla coherente abre con un propósito claro, desarrolla dos o tres razones en orden y cierra reuniéndolas.

nota.es: Se comprueba con las señales de orden: first, second, finally, to sum up.

items.texto: The second criterion is accuracy, and any shortcoming here, such as a slip in tense or a misused connector, is judged by how far it blurs the message.

traduccion.es: El segundo criterio es la precisión, y cualquier defecto aquí, como un desliz de tiempo o un conector mal usado, se juzga según cuánto difumina el mensaje.

nota.es: Un error que no impide entender pesa menos que uno que cambia el sentido.

items.texto: Tact is the third: a skilled speaker concedes a point and softens a request, and does not digress into blame or complaint.

traduccion.es: El tacto es el tercero: quien habla con habilidad concede un punto y suaviza una petición, y no se desvía hacia el reproche o la queja.

nota.es: Much as…, I was wondering whether… y should it fail son señales de tacto.

items.texto: The fourth criterion is evidence: a speaker who can cite a survey, a figure or a precise example is harder to ignore than one who says that many people agree.

traduccion.es: El cuarto criterio es la evidencia: quien puede citar una encuesta, una cifra o un ejemplo preciso es más difícil de ignorar que quien dice que mucha gente está de acuerdo.

nota.es: Una encuesta, una cifra o un ejemplo concreto valen más que «todo el mundo lo piensa».

items.texto: A fair verdict names a strength and a weakness, and it quotes the exact words that prove each one.

traduccion.es: Un veredicto justo nombra una fortaleza y una debilidad, y cita las palabras exactas que prueban cada una.

nota.es: Sin la cita exacta, una valoración es solo una opinión.

Good writers add nuance without losing their stance: I would argue that remote work helps, at least for tasks that hinge on concentration.

I would argue that a four-day week is worth trying, at least in offices. A company I know of tried it for six months, and the number of people off sick fell by a third. Admittedly, some customers may be disappointed to find the doors closed on Fridays. Even so, that cost is small beside the gain in the mood of the staff. Or rather, it is small if the company explains the change in advance. I have noticed that plans of this kind work best when the staff help to design them. Overall, then, I would not insist on the scheme for every firm, but I would certainly let firms experiment.

I would argue that a city should close its centre to cars, at least on weekends and in the busiest streets. Take my own town: two years ago the main square was full of traffic, and the shopkeepers used to complain that nobody could stop to look at the windows. Once the square became pedestrian, the shops gradually received more visitors, and the noise dropped noticeably. Admittedly, a ban is not free of problems, because older residents may find it harder to reach the centre and some deliveries may arrive late. Much as I accept that risk, I believe it is smaller than it looks, since a free bus and a few parking spaces at the edge can cover most needs. Or rather, it is smaller when the council consults the residents in advance. What I mean is that the plan hinges on preparation, not on enthusiasm. Every choice has a downside, but this one can sway even a sceptical shopkeeper if the trial is honest and limited. On balance, I would propose a six-month experiment, and I would revise the decision calmly once the figures are in.

texto.es: La práctica integrada final pide una respuesta completa en poco tiempo. Dedica un minuto a un esquema y sigue este orden: postura matizada (I would argue that…), ejemplo concreto (For example, …), concesión breve (Admittedly, … / Much as…), refutación (Even so, …), autocorrección visible (or rather, …) y cierre (On balance, …). Reserva el último minuto para revisar tiempos, conectores y tono. Con 240–300 palabras cabe todo, pero solo si cada frase cumple una función.

items.audio: I would argue that a four-day week is worth trying, at least in offices. A company I know of tried it for six months, and the number of people off sick fell by a third. Admittedly, some customers may be disappointed to find the doors closed on Fridays. Even so, that cost is small beside the gain in the mood of the staff. Or rather, it is small if the company explains the change in advance. I have noticed that plans of this kind work best when the staff help to design them. Overall, then, I would not insist on the scheme for every firm, but I would certainly let firms experiment.

items.respuesta: I would argue that a city should close its centre to cars, at least on weekends and in the busiest streets. Take my own town: two years ago the main square was full of traffic, and the shopkeepers used to complain that nobody could stop to look at the windows. Once the square became pedestrian, the shops gradually received more visitors, and the noise dropped noticeably. Admittedly, a ban is not free of problems, because older residents may find it harder to reach the centre and some deliveries may arrive late. Much as I accept that risk, I believe it is smaller than it looks, since a free bus and a few parking spaces at the edge can cover most needs. Or rather, it is smaller when the council consults the residents in advance. What I mean is that the plan hinges on preparation, not on enthusiasm. Every choice has a downside, but this one can sway even a sceptical shopkeeper if the trial is honest and limited. On balance, I would propose a six-month experiment, and I would revise the decision calmly once the figures are in.

Or rather, it is smaller when the council consults the residents in advance. What I mean is that the plan hinges on preparation, not on enthusiasm. Every choice has a downside, but this one can sway even a sceptical shopkeeper if the trial is honest and limited. On balance, I would propose a six-month experiment, and I would revise the decision calmly once the figures are in.

In my opinion, closing the city centre to cars is worth a serious trial, especially on the streets where people already walk more than they drive. Consider my aunt's bakery: two years ago the customers used to complain about the noise, and the drivers would park in front of the door for an hour. After the street became pedestrian, the bakery sold more, and the pavement was full of families. It is true that a few elderly customers were unhappy at first, because they could not get close by car. Even though that problem is real, I think it is easy to solve with a free bus and a few parking spaces nearby. To put it more precisely, the real difficulty is not the missing road but the lack of preparation. Let me rephrase that: a car-free centre works only when everyone knows how to arrive. Admittedly, not every street can be closed, and a hospital cannot be cut off. Still, many centres could. All in all, the evidence I have seen points to a modest but clear benefit, and I would support a trial.

Years ago, I used to believe that I would never speak English well. I had never spoken with a stranger in English, and I was afraid of making mistakes. Then I started studying with an app every morning, and in hindsight that routine was the start of my journey. The article says that students who learn with apps never speak fluently. Admittedly, an app alone may not be enough: it cannot give you a real conversation. Much as I respect the author, I would argue that the claim is too strong. The source seems to rely on a small survey, and its evidence looks anecdotal, so its conclusion may not be reliable. I was wondering whether the author could explain how many students took part. I understand that a short article has little space, and I appreciate the concern about speaking well. Revision: I first wrote that apps are useless for speaking, or rather, I should say that they are useful but not enough. On balance, the best plan is an app plus real conversations, and that is exactly what this course has given me, so I feel confident now.

When I was a child, I would watch films in English without understanding a word, and my cousin used to laugh at me. Later, I had to take an exam, and that was the moment when I decided to learn properly. An online post claims that apps are a waste of time and that nobody learns to speak with them. In the end, I changed my opinion only a little, and this course helped me to explain why.
